summary: Mobile Navigation Problem with WordPress 7.1
_description:
//English (Google Translate)//

Title:
Mobile Navigation: All submenus appear permanently open (WordPress 7.1). Simple overlay

Description:
After updating to WordPress 7.1, all navigation submenus appear permanently open in the mobile view when the hamburger menu is opened.

Behavior:
- Desktop: Works correctly
- Mobile (< 782px): When the hamburger menu is opened, all submenus become visible and remain open
- Clicks on submenu items work, but all submenus are visible simultaneously

Cause:
The element `.wp-block-navigation__submenu-container` has the attribute `data-wp-on--focus="actions.openMenuOnFocus"`. The Interactivity API opens all submenus simultaneously instead of controlling them individually.

----

//(Original German)//

Titel:
Mobile Navigation: Alle Submenüs werden permanent geöffnet angezeigt (WordPress 7.1). Einfaches Overlay

Beschreibung:
Nach Update auf WordPress 7.1 werden in der mobilen Ansicht alle Submenüs der Navigation permanent als geöffnet angezeigt, wenn das Hamburger-Menü geöffnet wird.

Verhalten:
- Desktop: funktioniert korrekt
- Mobile (< 782px): Beim Öffnen des Hamburger-Menüs werden alle Submenüs sichtbar und bleiben offen
- Klicks auf Submenü-Items funktionieren, aber alle sind gleichzeitig sichtbar

Ursache:
Das Element `.wp-block-navigation__submenu-container` hat das Attribut `data-wp-on--focus="actions.openMenuOnFocus"`. Die Interactivity API öffnet alle Submenüs gleichzeitig, statt sie individuell zu steuern.

Theme: Twenty-Twenty-five and Own Child-Theme
Browser: [Chrome Mobile]

summary: Block Supports: Allow CSS custom properties in wp_sanitize_block_gap_value()
_description:
When a theme defines a preset block gap in theme.json (such as styles.spacing.blockGap: "var:preset|spacing|32"):

1. wp_get_global_styles() resolves the preset to its CSS variable format: var(--wp--preset--spacing--32).
2. Candidate values for the global block gap in layout rendering are passed through wp_sanitize_block_gap_value().
3. Because wp_sanitize_block_gap_value() disallows parentheses to prevent CSS injection, the resolved preset is rejected and returns null.
4. As a result, Grid layout calculations in wp_get_layout_style() fall back to 0.5em instead of using the theme's preset gap value.
5. In Grid blocks with columnCount and minimumColumnWidth, columns stack into a single column.

Fix: Allow valid CSS custom property references matching `/^var\(--[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+\)$/`.

Gutenberg PR: https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/82817

summary: Many PHPUnit tests are not well isolated
_description:
In talking about tests at WCUS 2026, we reminded ourselves that many of our PHPUnit tests leak state and/or depend on previously leaked state. This is easy to see by running the tests in an arbitrary order:

{{{
npm run test:php -- --order-by=random
}}}

This lack of isolation can result in varied problems:
* A test cannot be run by itself
* A test class cannot be run by itself
* A test passes because of some previously leaked state and not because the test is actually testing the correct thing
* etc.

Reducing state leaking reduces fragility, increases confidence that tests are testing what they should be testing, and is a likely prerequisite for future parallel test running.

This ticket is for sharing a grab-bag of unrelated test fixes we worked on during WCUS.

summary: Customizer "Close" button returns to the upload-theme confirmation screen after a theme ZIP update, causing a "Please select a file to upload" error
_description:
**Steps to reproduce**
1. Go to Appearance > Themes > Add New > Upload Theme.
2. Upload a ZIP file for a theme that is already installed (same slug), and confirm the "Replace current with uploaded" / overwrite prompt.
3. On the resulting confirmation screen (URL pattern: wp-admin/update.php?action=upload-theme&package=<id>&overwrite=update-theme&_wpnonce=...), click "Customize" (or "Live Preview") to open the Customizer directly from that screen.
4. Inside the Customizer, click the Close (X) button / back arrow to return to the admin.

**Expected behavior**
The Customizer should return to a valid, reusable admin screen – e.g. the Themes overview (themes.php), similar to the existing fallback added in #46686 for a return URL that belongs to an inactive theme.

**Actual behavior**
The Customizer navigates back to the exact upload-confirmation URL it was opened from (update.php?action=upload-theme&overwrite=update-theme&package=...). Because this URL is normally only valid as the result of a POST request that included the uploaded file, reloading it via a plain GET request (as the Customizer's close action does) re-triggers the upload-theme handler without any file attached, which then shows the core error message "Please select a file to upload." (German: "Wähle bitte eine Datei.") instead of returning the admin to a usable screen.

**Notes**
- This looks closely related to #46686 ("Customize Close Button Not Updating URL", fixed in 5.4 via changeset 46754), which added a fallback to the Themes screen when the Customizer's stored return URL points to a page that is no longer valid for the active theme. That fix does not appear to cover this case, since the upload-theme confirmation URL is technically still "allowed" (the current user has access to it) – it simply isn't meant to be reloaded as a bare GET request.
- A possible fix: when the Customizer is opened directly from the upload-theme confirmation screen, store the Themes overview (themes.php) as the return URL instead of the confirmation screen's own URL – consistent with the existing fallback logic from #46686.

**Environment**
WordPress version: 7.1.4
Browser: Microsoft Edge 156.0.4314.50
Theme used to reproduce: any theme that supports the Customizer (reproduced with a custom theme; should be theme-independent since the bug is in wp-admin core, not in any theme code)
Multisite: no

summary: metadata registered using register_meta() do not persist through several tests
Reassess the need for the external-http tests
_description:
Tests in the `external-http` group are flakey because they rely on actual network requests over HTTP. There's no mocking in place. Server errors (HTTP 5XX) and more recently an increase in the frequency of HTTP 429 responses from wordpress.org will cause the tests to fail.

Let's reassess the tests in this group and question exactly what it is that each test is asserting.

As an example, the `Tests_HTTP_Functions::test_head_404()` test performs a HEAD request to a non-existent URL and then verifies that the response is not a `WP_Error` and that the response code is `404`.

What ''exactly'' is this verifying though?

* If it's verifying the correct population of the HTTP response code then that should be handled by test coverage on `WP_HTTP_Requests_Response` and a mocked up `\WpOrg\Requests\Response` instance. No need to perform a real HTTP request.
* If it's verifying specifically that a 404 response doesn't result in a `WP_Error` instance being returned by `wp_remote_*()` then can we do that without performing an actual HTTP request? It should be possible with a test-only transport class which returns a mocked raw HTTP response.

Of course we need to be careful not to remove or reduce coverage where it's needed, but I'm positive we can remove many of the actual HTTP requests from these tests (and move them out of the `external-http` group).

summary: Database tests fail on MariaDB 13.1 because utf8 now resolves to utf8mb4
_description:
Reported by @danielblack in [https://wordpress.slack.com/archives/C02RQBWTW/p1788847795453089 core Slack].

MariaDB 13.1.1 removes UTF8_IS_UTF8MB3 from the default old_mode ([https://jira.mariadb.org/browse/MDEV-30041 MDEV-30041]), so the charset name utf8 now means utf8mb4 instead of utf8mb3 in DDL and SET NAMES. This breaks 4 tests in Tests_DB_Charset (seen on MariaDB's own [https://buildbot.mariadb.org/#/builders/505/builds/8348/steps/4/logs/stdio WordPress buildbot]): test_get_table_charset, test_get_column_charset, test_strip_invalid_text_from_query, and test_set_charset_changes_the_connection_collation. 

They fail because the test file's $utf8_is_utf8mb3 flag (tests/phpunit/tests/db/charset.php:62-66) is set by a version check ("MariaDB ≥ 10.6.1"), which only accounts for the 10.6 change in how the server reports the charset, not the 13.1 change in what the name utf8 creates. Core's runtime is fine — wpdb::determine_charset() has upgraded utf8 to utf8mb4 since 4.6 — this is purely a test-expectation fix.

summary: Response from media library API query includes an empty array rather than an empty object
_description:
In the response to a media library query over the REST API, I am seeing that $wpimage->media_details->sizes is an empty array when there are no sizes, rather than an empty object (as a non-empty instance is an object). This discrepancy is inconsistent and breaks my recipient code. It's characteristic of json_encode being used on a keyed PHP array, when it can't tell the difference between keys and numeric indexes when empty.

I asked claude.ai to locate the bug to make it easy for you to fix. It agreed with my diagnosis and said:

File: wp-includes/rest-api/endpoints/class-wp-rest-attachments-controller.php

Method: prepare_item_for_response()

The bug: when wp_get_attachment_metadata() returns metadata with an empty sizes array (image too small for sub-sizes), the method populates `$data['media_details']` from that metadata but never explicitly sets `$data['media_details']['sizes']` to new stdClass. The `else { $data['media_details']['sizes'] = new stdClass; }` branch is only reached when $metadata itself is empty/falsy. The result is that sizes is either absent or an empty PHP array `[]` in the JSON output, rather than `{}`.

Prior art: reference Trac #51393, which addressed a related inconsistency but didn't fix this code path.

Your fix suggestion: initialise `$data['media_details']['sizes']` to `new stdClass` (or cast with (object)) before the loop that populates it, so the empty case is covered unconditionally.

summary: Twenty Twenty: Fix post meta wrapper not rendering when action hooks add custom content without the default meta
_description:
There’s a bug in the Twenty Twenty theme in `twentytwenty_get_post_meta`. The bug prevents the action hooks `twentytwenty_start_of_post_meta_list` and `twentytwenty_end_of_post_meta_list` from displaying additional meta data when the default meta data fields are not populated.

The variable `$has_meta` must be true for any meta to be displayed. It is set to `false` initially and is only set to `true` if one of the default meta are provided. For `single-bottom`, if no tags are in the post, `$has_meta` will be false regardless of additional meta attempting to be displayed by the action hooks.

I solved the bug by defining `$has_meta` as a global inside `twentytwenty_get_post_meta`. From there, I was able to modify its value to true within my action hook function.

Hope this can be fixed in the published version of the theme so I don’t have to use a hacked version.

I posted on the theme support page and was asked to post a bug in this forum instead. Link to my theme support post: [https://wordpress.org/support/topic/twentytwenty_end_of_post_meta_list-needs-global-has_meta/]

summary: Docblock improvements for 7.2
wp_read_audio_metadata() keeps no tags from FLAC, Ogg or M4A files
_description:
`wp_add_id3_tag_data()` reads tags only from ID3. FLAC and Ogg files store tags as Vorbis comments, and M4A files as QuickTime atoms, so these files keep no title, artist, album, year or track number.

=== Steps to reproduce ===

{{{
ffmpeg -f lavfi -i anullsrc -t 1 -metadata title=Test -metadata artist=Band t.flac
ffmpeg -f lavfi -i anullsrc -t 1 -metadata title=Test -metadata artist=Band t.mp3
}}}

Upload both and compare `wp_get_attachment_metadata()`. The MP3 has `title` and `artist`; the FLAC has neither. Reproduces on trunk with no plugins active.

=== Proposed fix ===

When a file has no ID3 tags, read the first tag set in `$data['tags']`, renaming keys to their ID3 names:

||= Vorbis / QuickTime =||= ID3 =||
|| `albumartist`, `album_artist` || `band` ||
|| `date`, `creation_date` || `year` ||
|| `tracknumber` || `track_number` ||
|| `discnumber`, `disc_number` || `part_of_a_set` ||
|| `lyrics` || `unsynchronised_lyric` ||

ID3 takes precedence when both exist, and tags never replace what was read from the stream, such as its encoder.

Send email notification when an application password is added
_description:
When the account password or email address of a user is changed (either by the user themselves or by an administrator) an email gets sent to the email address of the user informing them of the change. This email helps prevent a user account takeover from going unnoticed.

No such email is sent when an application password is added to a user's account. An application password is almost as privileged as the user's main password as it can be used to perform actions via the REST API, even though it can't be used to log in to wp-admin.

An email should be sent to the user when an application password is added to their account. If the creation of the application password is unexpected then this informs the user about it.

Web services such as GitHub send an email to a user informing them about newly granted access to their account for third party apps. The wording of the email sent by WordPress could be similar, framing it as an app now having access via a newly created application password. One important difference is that the name of the application password is controlled by the user adding the password, unlike services where a third party app is prohibited from using a name that might imply that it's a first party connection. If an attacker adds an application password with the name "WordPress" or the name of the site itself, it would be confusing for the user to receive an email which says "WordPress now has access to your user account".

That's a long way of saying that we need to be careful of how this email is phrased.

Secrets API: Small hardening fixes for names, stack traces and the All Settings screen
_description:
Follow-up to #66187. Three small issues found while testing the Secrets API on 7.2-beta3-64990.

'''1. A name with a trailing newline passes validation.'''

`wp_secrets_validate_name()` checks each segment with `'/^[a-z0-9]([a-z0-9_-]*[a-z0-9])?$/'`. Without the `D` modifier, `$` also matches before a final newline, so `"test/key\n"` is valid. The options API trims option names, so `"test/key\n"` and `"test/key"` share one row. But each value is encrypted for its own name, so a write through one name breaks the other:

{{{#!php
<?php
var_dump( wp_secrets_validate_name( "test/key\n" ) ); // true
wp_set_secret( 'test/key', 'value-plain' );
wp_set_secret( "test/key\n", 'value-newline' );
wp_get_secret( 'test/key' ); // WP_Error secret_decryption_failed
}}}

Fix: use `\z` instead of `$`, or add the `D` modifier.

'''2. Secret values can appear in stack traces.'''

The `$value` parameters of `wp_set_secret()` and the functions it calls have no `#[\SensitiveParameter]`, so an exception thrown while saving a secret prints the start of the value in the trace (for example `wp_set_secret('test/key', 'sk-live-1234567...')`). Core already uses the attribute for passwords in `pluggable.php` and `class-wpdb.php`.

'''3. Settings > All Settings shows the root key as an editable field.'''

`wp-admin/options.php` lists `_wp_secrets_root_key` as a plain text field. Saving that screen with the field changed replaces the root key, and every stored secret becomes unreadable. Only administrators can reach the screen, but one mistaken save cannot be undone. `options.php` already masks `connectors_*_api_key` options and disables them; the root key could get the same treatment.

Use of AI tools: I used Claude Code to review the code. I reproduced 1 myself and checked 2 and 3 in the code.

summary: Secrets API: Site Health misreports the secrets backend and gives key advice that locks stored secrets
_description:
Follow-up to [64337] (#66187), found while testing 7.2-beta1.

'''1. Site Health advice that locks every stored secret.''' On a site without `WP_SECRETS_KEY`, the key source test says to "Define WP_SECRETS_KEY with a value from `wp secret generate-key`". That command is not in core or WP-CLI (the commands stayed in the feature plugin, per [64337]). Following the advice after any secret is stored makes every stored secret unreadable and blocks saving new ones, because the root key stays wrapped with the previous site key and nothing in core re-wraps it (`rotate_site_key()` has no caller). Site Health then reports the new key as good.

Reproduced on trunk:
 1. `wp_set_secret( 'test/api-key', 'value' )`, read back fine. Site Health: recommended, "Define WP_SECRETS_KEY with a value from `wp secret generate-key`".
 2. Define `WP_SECRETS_KEY` as a base64 random 32-byte value: `wp_get_secret()` returns `secret_key_unavailable`, `wp_set_secret()` fails too, and the key source test says "Secrets API is using a dedicated key" (good).
 3. Remove the constant: the secret reads back again.

This is the Site Health side of the risk @Clorith raised in #66187 comment:23 for salt rotation. It does not change the salt fallback itself.

'''2. A broken backend reads as healthy.''' The undecryptable and rotation tests turn the `WP_Error` from `wp_list_secrets()` into an empty result ("All secrets can be decrypted", "No secrets are pending rotation"). The key source test detects a broken `secrets.php` by matching "broken" in a translated string, so on translated sites it reports "using a dedicated key".

'''3. Provider drop-ins get the wrong advice.''' With a `secrets.php` that replaces the provider (a host KMS or vault), the key source test still describes the unused default keyring and recommends `WP_SECRETS_KEY`.

'''4. `secrets.php` is not listed as a drop-in.''' It loads on every request like `object-cache.php`, but `_get_dropins()` does not include it, so neither Plugins > Drop-ins nor Site Health Info shows it.

PRs: https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/14847 (1 to 3, one commit each) and https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/14848 (4).

AI assistance: Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5) for finding these, drafting the patches and tests, and running them. I reviewed the patches and reproduced the steps above on 7.2-beta1.

summary: Secrets API: A failed read of a secret's record reads as a missing secret
_description:
Follow-up to [64337] (#66187). Related: #66413.

`WP_Secrets_Option_Store::get()` reads a record with `get_option( $name, null )` (or `get_site_option()`). Those return the default both when the option doesn't exist and when the query fails. So a failed read, such as a killed query, a lost connection or a replica that is behind, looks like "this secret does not exist":

* `wp_get_secret()` returns `null` instead of `WP_Error`. That breaks the three-state contract, which reserves `null` for a secret that doesn't exist. A caller that sees `null` may ask for the credential again or create a new one.
* `wp_set_secret()` treats the secret as new. It returns `true` and writes a record with no previous version, so a rotation in progress loses the value it depends on.

#66413 is the same problem for the root key.

Reproduced on trunk, single site. The first SELECT of the record fails once, through a `query` filter:

{{{
before: current two, previous one
wp_get_secret() during a failed read: NULL
wp_set_secret( three ) during a failed read: true
after: current three, previous NULL
}}}

Possible fix: when `get_option()` returns the default, check against the database the way #66413's patch does for the root key. Return `secret_store_unavailable` if that read fails too. The write path already treats `secret_store_unavailable` from the store as fatal.

AI assistance: Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5) for finding this and writing the reproduction. I ran it and reviewed the results.

summary: Secrets API: A failed read of the root key replaces it, and every stored secret becomes unreadable
Secrets API: encrypted, versioned storage for credentials
_description:
The [https://make.wordpress.org/core/2026/08/25/proposal-a-secrets-api-for-wordpress-7-2/ Secrets API proposal] is for a core API that stores credentials such as API keys and tokens encrypted at rest, keeps a previous version for rotation, and lets hosts replace the storage through a `secrets.php` drop-in. This ticket covers the 7.2 part: the API itself. The admin screen is deferred to 7.3, as the proposal says. The WP-CLI commands stay in the feature plugin for now, since WP-CLI commands ship as WP-CLI packages rather than in core.

The patch is the `src/` directory of the [https://github.com/ericmann/secrets-api feature plugin], copied without changes, plus the wiring the plugin's bootstrap does today. The plugin has been public since 4 September and is at v0.2.0. The documentation, including every place the code departs from the proposal and why, is at [https://secretsapi.dev/ secretsapi.dev].

This is also the storage #64789 asks for. The Connectors screen from #64730 keeps AI provider API keys as plaintext options, which are visible on `options.php`. Stored through this API, they are encrypted under a key that is not in the database, so a database dump or backup no longer exposes them. Moving Connectors onto `wp_set_secret()` and `wp_get_secret()` can follow once this lands.

=== The patch ===

 * **The API:** 14 new files in `src/wp-includes/`.
   * the public functions
   * `WP_Secret` and `WP_Secret_Version`
   * the provider, store and keyring interfaces, with their default and fail-closed implementations
   * the cipher and the key manager

   `src/wp-admin/includes/secrets-site-health.php` adds three Site Health tests and a debug-information section.
 * **Loading:** `wp-settings.php` loads the API, then loads `wp-content/secrets.php` through a new `wp_load_secrets_dropin()` in `load.php`, just before must-use plugins.
 * **Failing closed:** if the drop-in throws, or sets a provider, store or keyring that does not implement its interface, every Secrets API call returns `WP_Error` for the rest of the request. Nothing falls back to the default provider: a broken drop-in has to read as unreachable, never as "this secret does not exist". See [https://secretsapi.dev/decisions/0007-fail-closed-on-a-broken-drop-in/ ADR 0007].
 * **Capabilities:** `populate_roles_720()` grants `manage_secrets` to administrators on install, and `upgrade_720()` grants it on upgrade. `manage_network_secrets` joins the other network capabilities in `map_meta_cap()`, so only super admins hold it.
 * **Tests:** the plugin's tests for everything in `src/`, 371 of them, in `tests/phpunit/tests/secrets/`. They come with provider and keyring conformance suites for hosts that write drop-ins.

=== Changes and additions beyond the proposal ===

The proposal names `wp_set_secret()`, `wp_get_secret()`, `wp_delete_secret()`, `wp_import_option_as_secret()`, `WP_Secret`, and `WP_Secret_Version`. Everything below differs from or goes beyond that, and is listed so each item can be reviewed, and rejected, on its own. The reasoning for each is on the linked page.

 * `WP_Secret::reveal()` returns `string|WP_Error`, not `string`: [https://secretsapi.dev/spec/retrieval/ retrieval]
 * `wp_retire_secret_version()` and `wp_list_secrets()`: [https://secretsapi.dev/spec/rotation/ rotation], [https://secretsapi.dev/spec/retrieval/ retrieval]
 * Network scope, which the proposal describes without naming functions: `wp_set_network_secret()`, `wp_get_network_secret()`, `wp_delete_network_secret()`, `wp_retire_network_secret_version()`, `wp_list_network_secrets()`. See [https://secretsapi.dev/spec/network/ network].
 * `wp_secrets_validate_name()`, `wp_secrets_memzero()`, `wp_using_secrets_dropin()`, `wp_secrets_provider_is_writable()`, `wp_secrets_provider_label()`
 * The `wp_secret_changed` action, for auditing, plus `WP_Secret::get_name()` and `WP_Secret::withheld()`
 * The `WP_Secrets_Provider`, `WP_Secrets_Store`, and `WP_Secrets_Keyring` interfaces, and their default and fail-closed implementations. The provider replaced the proposal's two-part drop-in contract after hosts on the proposal thread showed it could not describe how they already deploy. See [https://secretsapi.dev/spec/providers-and-keyrings/ providers and keyrings] and [https://secretsapi.dev/decisions/0001-provider-as-outermost-extension-point/ ADR 0001].
 * Constants: ten `WP_SECRETS_ERROR_*` codes, `WP_SECRETS_RECORD_VERSION`, `WP_SECRETS_MAX_NAME_LENGTH`, `WP_SECRETS_CAP_MANAGE`, and `WP_SECRETS_CAP_MANAGE_NETWORK`

The [https://secretsapi.dev/spec/scope/ scope page] has the complete list.

=== Testing ===

 * **In this branch:**
   * `npm run test:php -- --group secrets` passes on single site and multisite (371 tests each).
   * `tests/phpunit/tests/user/capabilities.php` passes with both capabilities added to its inventory.
   * The full single-site suite shows no new failures.
 * **The plugin's CI:** PHP 7.4, 8.0 and 8.3, each against WordPress latest and trunk, plus a multisite job and a WP-CLI smoke test on PHP 7.4 and 8.3.
 * **Drop-in examples:** the ones in the plugin's `examples/` directory have been run against live AWS KMS and AWS Secrets Manager, against HashiCorp Vault 2.1.1 (including a sealed server), and against OpenBao 2.7.0.

=== Notes for committers ===

 * `$wp_db_version` is set to a placeholder, 61900, which `upgrade_720()` checks. It needs the real revision number on commit.
 * `wp-tests-config-sample.php` ships placeholder salts, and the default keyring deliberately refuses to derive a key from them. When the salts are placeholders, the test bootstrap therefore defines a fixed `WP_SECRETS_KEY` in the main PHPUnit process. The four tests that exercise the salt-based fallback are skipped in that case.
 * Every new symbol is marked `@since 7.2.0`.

summary: Secrets API: Generate `WP_SECRETS_KEY` during installation so secrets do not depend on the salts
_description:
Follow-up to [64337] (#66187). See #66380.

When `WP_SECRETS_KEY` is not defined, the Secrets API derives its key from `LOGGED_IN_KEY` and `LOGGED_IN_SALT`. Rotating the salts is common advice (`wp config shuffle-salts`, security plugins), and before 7.2 it only logged users out. On a site using that fallback it now makes every stored secret unreadable, and blocks saving new ones, until the old values are restored. #66187 comment:23 raised this, and comment:24 confirmed it on 7.2-beta2. #66380 fixes what Site Health says about it. This ticket removes the dependency for new installs.

=== Proposed fix ===

`setup-config.php` already generates the eight keys and salts. It should also write a `WP_SECRETS_KEY` define after them: a base64-encoded random 32-byte value, which is the form the Secrets API uses as raw key material. New installs then never use the fallback, and rotating the salts leaves their secrets readable.

=== Notes ===

* `wp-config-sample.php` stays unchanged on purpose. The Secrets API rejects the salt placeholder, but it accepts any `WP_SECRETS_KEY` string, so a placeholder in the sample would give every hand-edited install that left it alone the same public key. A site whose config was copied from the sample by hand keeps the salt fallback, and Site Health recommends a dedicated key.
* Without a CSPRNG, `setup-config.php` leaves the define out rather than fall back to `wp_generate_password()` or the secret-key API, and the site uses the salt fallback.
* Existing sites are not affected. Moving one off the fallback means re-wrapping the root key, which core has no public path for yet (planned for 7.3).
* Installers that write `wp-config.php` themselves, such as WP-CLI's `wp config create` and hosts' one-click installers, are out of scope here, but should do the same.

AI assistance: Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5) for drafting the patch and this ticket. I reviewed both.

summary: Backport removal of 1024-bit root certificates to older branches
_description:
In [61669] (#64063) the legacy 1024-bit root certificates were removed from `ca-bundle.crt`. The older branches still include them.

These certs were only kept for OpenSSL 1.0.1e to 1.0.1q, which had path discovery bugs (see #34935). Those versions are over a decade old.

=== 6.8 and 6.9

These branches build the bundle with Grunt. The backport is:

 * Apply the `Gruntfile.js` change from [61669]
 * Delete `wp-includes/certificates/cacert.pem` and `wp-includes/certificates/legacy-1024bit.pem`
 * Regenerate `ca-bundle.crt`

=== 4.7 to 6.7

These branches have no Grunt task for certs, `ca-bundle.crt` is maintained directly. The backport is to copy over trunk's `ca-bundle.crt`.

Add an index for get_lastpostmodified query
_description:
I had a friend (Jools Wills) look over a WordPress site recently, to get a fresh view on what might be optimised, and he noticed a query which might benefit from an additional index on `WP_Posts`. The query `SELECT post_modified_gmt FROM $wpdb->posts WHERE post_status = 'publish' AND post_type = 'post' ORDER BY post_modified_gmt DESC LIMIT 1` in `get_lastpostmodified` is run for last modified date in GMT, and currently doesn't use an index. This SQL is run whenever certain types of feed are requested as far as I can see.

We added `CREATE INDEX type_status_modified ON wp_posts (post_type, post_status, post_modified_gmt);` and `CREATE INDEX type_status_modified_no_id ON wp_posts (post_type, post_status, post_date_gmt);` and the query runs a lot faster now. The following timings were taken running the first query (`post_modified_gmt`) on a 36,362 row posts table. Note that it doesn't use filesort after the index has been added.

''Before:''

{{{
mysql> EXPLAIN SELECT post_modified_gmt FROM slgr_posts WHERE post_status = 'publish' AND post_type = 'post' ORDER BY post_modified_gmt DESC LIMIT 1;
+----+-------------+------------+------+------------------+------------------+---------+-------------+-------+-----------------------------+
| id | select_type | table      | type | possible_keys    | key              | key_len | ref         | rows  | Extra                       |
+----+-------------+------------+------+------------------+------------------+---------+-------------+-------+-----------------------------+
|  1 | SIMPLE      | slgr_posts | ref  | type_status_date | type_status_date | 124     | const,const | 24718 | Using where; Using filesort |
+----+-------------+------------+------+------------------+------------------+---------+-------------+-------+-----------------------------+
1 row in set (0.03 sec)
}}}


 * 0.21290683746338ms
 * 0.25690102577209ms
 * 0.230553150177ms
 * 0.2274341583252ms
 * 0.23083996772766ms

''After:''

{{{
mysql> EXPLAIN SELECT post_modified_gmt FROM slgr_posts WHERE post_status = 'publish' AND post_type = 'post' ORDER BY post_modified_gmt DESC LIMIT 1;
+----+-------------+------------+------+---------------------------------------+----------------------+---------+-------------+-------+-------------+
| id | select_type | table      | type | possible_keys                         | key                  | key_len | ref         | rows  | Extra       |
+----+-------------+------------+------+---------------------------------------+----------------------+---------+-------------+-------+-------------+
|  1 | SIMPLE      | slgr_posts | ref  | type_status_date,type_status_modified | type_status_modified | 124     | const,const | 24718 | Using where |
+----+-------------+------------+------+---------------------------------------+----------------------+---------+-------------+-------+-------------+
1 row in set (0.00 sec)
}}}

 * 0.00082707405090332ms
 * 0.00072288513183594ms
 * 0.00074386596679688ms
 * 0.00066494941711426ms
 * 0.00066208839416504ms

In `get_lastpostmodified` both these queries are run, so the total savings in my case on a quiet server are nearly 0.5 seconds... worth having, I reckon.

summary: "Attach to existing content" modal shows posts and pages of other users
_description:
From the Media library, a user can attach media (through the Attach link) that were uploaded by himself only. The first image shows the Attach links appearing for certain media only.

In the same way, the "Attach to existing content" should also list only those posts/pages for which the user has the permissions to attach.

Instead it lists all posts (including private) and pages of all users, and then, upon selection, gives the message "Sorry, you are not allowed to edit this post."

summary: Add end-to-end tests for wp-admin screens
_description:
#49507 adds e2e tests for the edit posts page. The goal is to write tests for all the admin, but we should be clear on which parts need most testing and what exactly to test. To kick things off, I'm making a list of all the pages, some of the tests we should write, and some questions that occurred to me. Feedback on what to add, change or remove is very welcome!

Dashboard:
* Quick draft section: add title, save draft, navigate to posts page and check it's there.

Updates page: not sure how we should test this one.

Categories:
* Add new category: add name, click add new category button, check if it appears in list
* Check that bulk deleting all categories leaves “uncategorized” untouched
* Add child category
* Delete category
* Search for category
* Search for non-existing category

Tags: same as categories.

Media:
* Add image to library
* Edit image alt text, title, desc
* Search for image
* Search for non-existing image

Pages: same as posts (see #49507)

Comments:
* Create post, view it, add a comment, check that it displays in comments page.

Themes:
* Search for a theme
* Activate a theme
* Delete a theme, then search for it
* Add new theme and activate it

Customize: this is pretty theme-dependent, so we should pick a theme and check a few flows on it.

Widgets and Menus: might not be worth writing tests yet as these screens are being re-written.

Theme editor:
* Add a line of CSS in the theme stylesheet and check for it in the front end?

Plugins: how should we test this page?

Users:
* Add new user
* Search for user 
* change user role
* Check admin user can't change itself to subscriber

Profile: there are lots of options here, should we test changes to each of them? Some may not be relevant, e.g. profile pic just takes us to Gravatar.

Import: We could test whether the plugins install correctly, but any further than that should be unnecessary (the plugins should have their own tests)

Export/Export personal data: would it be worth trying to check the contents of the downloaded files? 

Site health: there's no real interaction on this page, so maybe we can skip it.

Erase personal data: not sure how to test this one.

Settings: like profile, lots of options here. Test each individually?

summary: Installation Tests: single-site installs of 5.9 and 6.0 fatal on a truncated Twenty Twenty-Two pattern file
_description:
Since [63517] added a post-install smoke check to the Installation Tests workflow, single-site installs of WordPress 5.9 and 6.0 fatal. Multisite skips the smoke check, so it passes.

Example, WP 5.9.20: https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/actions/runs/40768551377

{{{
require(): Failed opening required '.../wp-content/themes/twentytwentytwo/inc/patterns/header-text-only-with-tagline-black-background.php'
}}}

The file is in the release packages. The workflow downloads with `wp core download`, which fetches the tarball. WP-CLI 2.12.0, the version setup-php installs, extracts tarballs with `PharData` first ([https://github.com/wp-cli/wp-cli/blob/v2.12.0/php/WP_CLI/Extractor.php Extractor.php]). `PharData` cuts this file's 107-character path at 100 characters, so it lands as `…black-backgro` with no `.php`.

Before [63517], the install tests stopped at `wp core install` and never loaded the theme, so this was never seen.

WP-CLI's main branch now runs `tar xz` first and falls back to `PharData` only on error, but no release CI uses includes that yet.

Possible fixes:

 1. Download the tarball and extract it with the system `tar` in `install-testing.yml`.
 2. Move CI to a WP-CLI release that includes the `tar xz`-first change, once one ships.

Follow-up to #66036.

E2E tests: run the Playwright suite in parallel
_description:
The end-to-end test suite runs every test on a single Playwright worker, so its
wall-clock time grows with each spec added. It now holds 101 tests across 24 spec
files and takes about 5 minutes. CI runs the whole suite twice, once with
`SCRIPT_DEBUG` on and once off, each under a 20-minute job timeout.

This is a good time to set up a parallel run suite that uses more Playwright workers, a set a good practices model before new specs are added.

High level plan:

 * '''Split the suite.''' The specs that make the site unusable run on their own. Everything else runs in parallel.
 * '''Isolate the test data.''' Each test creates the posts, pages, media, terms and users it needs and deletes them afterwards, instead of clearing shared data or reading unfiltered admin lists. Some specs already do this and are the model for the rest.
 * '''Use test locks for what is left.''' A few tests read a site-wide list or change a site setting, and no amount of isolation makes them safe side by side. Named locks keep only those tests apart, rather than making the whole suite serial. Playwright 1.64 supports locks and is already in place.

summary: Build/Test Tools: Skip the WordPress install in process-isolated tests
_description:
Tests marked `@runInSeparateProcess` load `tests/phpunit/includes/bootstrap.php` again in a child process, and every child reruns `install.php`, dropping and recreating all tables. The parent process has already installed WordPress before the first test runs, so the reinstall only adds time to each isolated test. There are 115 isolated test methods in 40 files (138 child processes per run, counting data sets), up from 39 at the start of October 2026.

The proposed change skips the install when `$GLOBALS['__PHPUNIT_BOOTSTRAP']` is set. PHPUnit sets that global only while a child process loads the bootstrap, and the bootstrap already uses it for `WP_SECRETS_KEY`. `WP_TESTS_SKIP_INSTALL=1` keeps working as before.

The reinstall was also hiding state that test classes leak: whenever an isolated test ran between a leaking class and one that needed clean state, the reinstall reset it. Without it, several leaks surfaced in CI, e.g.:

 * `customize/custom-css-setting.php` grants super admin to a fixture user and never revokes it, breaking `Tests_Multisite_wpMsUsersListTable::test_get_views_should_return_views_by_default`.
 * `feed/rss2.php` and `feed/atom.php` delete `blogdescription` on class tear down, so the regenerated `tests/qunit/fixtures/wp-api-generated.js` differs from the committed one.
 * With a persistent object cache, a rolled back test's values stay in the cache until the next `set_up()`. An isolated test boots WordPress in between and acts on them outside any transaction, e.g. a rolled back `theme_switched` makes `init` rebuild and commit the sidebars, breaking `Tests_WP_Customize_Manager::test_wp_customize_publish_changeset` in the memcached job.

Instead of fixing each leak per test, `WP_UnitTestCase_Base` now resets the shared state itself:

 * `set_up_before_class()` snapshots the options table once, then starts each class from fresh-install data (`_delete_all_data()` and a cache flush), so an isolated test doesn't collide with fixtures the parent committed.
 * `tear_down_after_class()` flushes the cache before the cleanup and restores the options snapshot after it.
 * `_delete_all_data()` drops deleted users from `site_admins` and updates the network user counts on multisite.
 * `tear_down()` flushes a persistent object cache right after the rollback.

Locally (Docker, PHPUnit 9.6, no coverage, median of 5 rounds), the 40ed tests went from 301s to 141s on single site and from 569s to 107s on multisite, with the same results. The coverage job should gain the most, since each reinstall is slowest there.

summary: Plugins: Preflight activation to avoid WSOD when plugin code uses syntax incompatible with PHP runtime
_description:
Problem
-------
Activating a plugin whose code is valid only on newer PHP versions (for example, using `false` as a return type in PHP 8.3) on a site running an older PHP version (e.g. PHP 8.0) can produce a fatal parse error. Because the plugin can already be persisted as "active" before compatibility is verified, the site can end up in a broken/white-screen state that requires DB or filesystem access to recover.

Steps to reproduce
------------------
1. On a site running PHP 8.0, install a plugin whose main file uses syntax valid in PHP 8.3 (e.g., `function foo(): false {}`).
2. Attempt to activate the plugin via wp-admin → Plugins → Activate.
3. The site will display a fatal parse error and the plugin will be in the active_plugins list, causing further loads to attempt to include it.

Expected
--------
Plugin activation should perform a preflight check and not persist a plugin as active if its main file produces a fatal/parsing error. A failed activation should abort and leave the active_plugins option unchanged.

Proposed solution
-----------------
Before updating `active_plugins`, preflight-load the plugin main file (sandboxed). If loading produces a fatal error (parse or otherwise), abort activation and show the error without saving the plugin as active. Implementation changes are proposed in:
- `src/wp-admin/includes/plugin.php` (inside `activate_plugin()`)
- Unit tests added in `tests/phpunit/tests/admin/includesPlugin.php`

Patch/PR
-------
A PR is available on GitHub and this ticket will include the patch. Please see linked PR for details.

Environment tested
------------------
- WordPress: <trunk>
- PHP: 8.3 (plugin syntax that causes repro)
- OS: Windows 11
- Browser: Google Chrome

Font Library: TTF uploads are rejected when fileinfo reports font/ttf
_description:
`WP_Font_Utils::get_allowed_font_mime_types()` expects TrueType fonts to be detected as `font/sfnt`. libmagic reports them as `font/ttf` since file 5.47 (https://github.com/file/file/commit/6481672a8e), so `wp_check_filetype_and_ext()` rejects the upload with `rest_font_upload_invalid_file_type`.

This affects PHP builds that use a newer libmagic: PHP 8.6 bundles libmagic 5.48, and distribution builds that link the system libmagic can be affected on older PHP versions too.

Results for `tests/phpunit/data/fonts/OpenSans-Regular.ttf`:

||= detector =||= result =||
|| PHP 8.5.12 `finfo` (bundled libmagic 5.46) || `font/sfnt` ||
|| upstream libmagic master (with the fix below) || `font/ttf` ||
|| PHP 8.6.0-dev `finfo` (bundled libmagic 5.48) || `application/octet-stream` ||

The `application/octet-stream` result on PHP 8.6 is an upstream libmagic regression, fixed in https://github.com/file/file/commit/ba72caa54b and reported to PHP in https://github.com/php/php-src/issues/25051. Once PHP takes that fix, TTF files are detected as `font/ttf`, and the upload is still rejected.

`Tests_REST_WpRestFontFacesController::test_create_item_with_multiple_font_files` fails on PHP 8.6.0-dev and passes on PHP 8.5.

Suggested fix: during font uploads, accept a `.ttf` file detected as either `font/sfnt` or `font/ttf`. A PHP version check alone would miss builds that use the system libmagic.

summary: `get_allowed_http_origins()` should not trust the insecure origin of an HTTPS site
_description:
The `get_allowed_http_origins()` function always adds both the `http://` and `https://` variants of the admin and home host to the allowed origins list, regardless of the site's scheme. On a site served only over HTTPS, the `http://` origin is therefore trusted even though the site doesn't use it.

This feeds `send_origin_headers()` which reflects a matching `Origin` into `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`. A network attacker who can tamper with plaintext HTTP traffic can issue a credentialed cross-origin request to the HTTPS site and read the response.

Fix: Add the `http://` origin only when the corresponding `admin_url()`/`home_url()` is not HTTPS.

Related: #43428 

Originally reported by talkemade on HackerOne.

Harden API requests against man-in-the-middle attacks
_description:
API requests are allowed over standard HTTP if SSL is not correctly configured on the server. That allows those servers to continue updating, rather than being stuck on an old (and potentially insecure) version (r25956).

Right now the downgrade triggers a PHP error, but users/devs will only know about it if they check the raw log files, since `WP_DEBUG_DISPLAY` is (hopefully) disabled on production servers. So users in this situation are mostly unaware of the server configuration errors, and the risks associated with unauthenticated API requests.

While it's good to avoid trapping them on older versions, there are a few things that we could consider to improve the mitigate the negative side-effects:

* Prompt the user to confirm they wish to continue making the request, even though it won't be secure. This would probably need to be paired with a page on the Codex explaining the problem, and giving them a message they can copy/paste to send to their hosting provider. Normally we would avoid burdening the user with technical details like this, but this instance might be worth an exception, given the security concerns? Maybe instead of linking to the Codex, we could build a user-friendly debugging/health-status page in Core?

* Only downgrade to HTTP for essential requests, like Core/plugin/theme updates. This would shrink the attack surface, but it may still be wide enough that it's not worth it hurting UX. Additionally, [https://core.trac.wordpress.org/ticket/42004 Events API requests could indirectly lead to users learning about best practices for picking a better host].

* Any other ideas?

_description:
`wp_get_l10n_php_file_data()` in `wp-includes/l10n.php` maps the PO headers it returns onto the keys a `.l10n.php` file stores them under:

{{{#!php
'PO-Revision-Date'   => 'po-revision-date',
}}}

No generated `.l10n.php` file uses that key. The revision date is written as `translation-revision-date`, so `PO-Revision-Date` always comes back empty.

`tests/phpunit/data/languages/de_CH.l10n.php` has the same wrong key, which is why the existing coverage in `Tests_L10n::test_wp_get_installed_translations_for_core()` passes. The fixture matches the code rather than a real file. `tests/phpunit/data/l10n/plural-complex.php`, added earlier in [57518], uses the correct key.

== Why it matters ==

`wp_get_installed_translations()` falls back to this reader when a translation has no sibling `.po` file. That value is sent to api.wordpress.org to work out which language packs are out of date. With an empty revision date, a pack that is already installed and current gets offered again.

Measured on trunk with the Twenty Twenty-Five nl_NL pack, freshly installed, changing nothing but whether the `.po` is on disk:

|| state || `wp_get_installed_translations()` reports || offers after `wp_update_themes()` ||
|| .po present || 2025-08-05 20:37:56+0000 || 0 ||
|| .po absent || empty string || 1 ||

== Fix ==

Read `translation-revision-date`, and correct the `de_CH.l10n.php` fixture to use it as well.

`POT-Creation-Date` maps to `pot-creation-date`, which no format writes, so it stays empty. Left alone here.

----

This came out of #65429 but is not the cause of that report, where the `.po` files were present. Filed separately since the defect stands on its own.

An earlier version of this description claimed the key had been renamed upstream. That was wrong, see comments below. The fixture was simply wrong from the start.

force_balance_tags() corrupts MathML saved by the Math block
_description:
== Description ==

When the `use_balanceTags` option is enabled, `balanceTags()` runs on `content_save_pre` and rewrites the MathML that the core Math block (`core/math`) stores in post content. The result is broken markup on the front end: fractions lose their numerator or denominator, and in the common case the whole expression is truncated after the first fraction containing a grouped sub-expression.

The cause is in `force_balance_tags()`. It only allows a short list of tags (`$nestable_tags`: `article`, `aside`, `blockquote`, `details`, `div`, `figure`, `object`, `q`, `section`, `span`) to be opened while the same tag is the innermost open tag. For any other tag it force-closes the outer element first. MathML nests `<mrow>` inside `<mrow>` all the time (every grouped sub-expression, every `\Delta`, `\mathbf{}`, `\left...\right`, and so on), so the balancer closes the outer `<mrow>` early and everything that follows is shifted up a level.

Because the Math block wraps the expression in `<semantics>`, and a `<semantics>` element only renders its first child, anything pushed out of the outer `<mrow>` becomes a later sibling and is treated as an annotation. The visible symptom is an equation that stops rendering part way through.

== Steps to reproduce ==

1. Enable the option. It is hidden from Settings → Writing on sites created after WordPress 4.3 (`initial_db_version >= 32453`), but still honoured:
{{{
wp option update use_balanceTags 1
}}}
   (or set it on `/wp-admin/options.php`)
2. Create a post, insert a Math block, and enter:
{{{
y = \frac{\Delta x}{t} + 1
}}}
3. Save the post and view it on the front end.

Expected: the fraction renders as Δx over t.



Actual: the page shows only `y = Δx`. The fraction bar is gone, because the `<mfrac>` now has three children and the browser falls back to laying them out in a row, and `t + 1` is not displayed at all.

== Markup ==

What the editor saves (abbreviated to the `<math>` contents):
{{{
<semantics>
  <mrow>
    <mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo>
    <mfrac>
      <mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow>
      <mi>t</mi>
    </mfrac>
    <mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn>
  </mrow>
  <annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = \frac{\Delta x}{t} + 1</annotation>
</semantics>
}}}

What `force_balance_tags()` turns it into:
{{{
<semantics>
  <mrow>
    <mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo>
    <mfrac>
      <mrow></mrow>
      <mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></mrow>
      <mi>x</mi>
    </mfrac>
  </mrow>
  <mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn>
  <annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = \frac{\Delta x}{t} + 1</annotation>
</semantics>
}}}

The inner `<mrow>` for `\Delta` triggers the "same tag already open" rule, so the balancer inserts `</mrow>` before it (the empty numerator). The original `</mrow>` that closed the numerator no longer matches, so the balancer walks the stack back to the outer `<mrow>` and closes `<mfrac>` and the outer `<mrow>` there. The denominator `t` and the trailing `+ 1` end up as siblings of the `<mrow>` inside `<semantics>`, where they are never rendered.

The same thing happens with any expression that produces an `<mrow>` directly inside an `<mrow>`, which the Math block's converter (temml) does for most non-trivial input.

----

I'm testing this on current trunk (ac530b68aa).
#66153 is somewhat related but isn't about the `use_balanceTags` option.

summary: Multiple runs of the Test Old Branches workflow in a short period of time can cause a stampede of automatic reruns and Slack notifications
_description:
GitHub Actions workflows are configured to automatically rerun when the first run attempt is cancelled or fails. They are also configured so that when the triggering event for a run is not `pull_request` the `concurrency.group` value is `WORKFLOWNAME-SHA`. Because old branches do not receive updates often, the runs triggered by `workflow_dispatch` usually have the same concurrency value for m any consecutive runs.

When the Test Old Branches workflow runs more than once in short period of time, this causes a cascade of cancellations, re-runs, and Slack notifications. Consider the following example:

- Commit made to `trunk` that runs Test Old Branches workflow.
- Run 1 starts
- Second commit made to `trunk` that runs Test Old Branches workflow.
- Run 2 starts
- Incomplete runs triggered by the first commit are cancelled based on the concurrency group
- Run 1 is restarted
- Incomplete runs triggered by the second commit are cancelled based on the concurrency group
- Run 2 is restarted
- Incomplete runs triggered by the first commit are cancelled for the second time based on the concurrency group
- Run 1 cancellations send a Slack notification to raise awareness.

This is then made worse because a successful run following a cancelled or failed run is considered "fixed", which is also a scenario where a Slack notification is pushed.

With 25+ branches eligible to receive security updates as a courtesy, this means that roughly 150 workflow runs are triggered every time the Test Old Branches workflow runs (using 25 branches * 6 workflows each, which is a rough average) and potentially roughly the same number of notifications for cancellations, then the same number for "fixes". This can be even worse if the commit made in `trunk` caused legitimate failures or also experienced timeouts/cancellations, and when a number of other commits are made around the same time.

The cancelled run Slack notification is configured to only send a notice for only the second run attempt to avoid needlessly sharing a timeout that resolves itself during the automatic re-run (see r62740). However, the `cancelled` outcome in GitHub Actions represents a few different outcomes that are not easy to clarify. A cancellation could be a timeout, a user initiated cancellation, a concurrency-based cancellation, and sometimes a platform-level problem can cause cancellations.

Because of this there's no logic included to determine if the cancellation was caused by the configured concurrency groupings, which is an expected and desired outcome and does not warrant a rerun or Slack notification.

[https://wordpress.slack.com/archives/C02RQBWTW/p1788446249310839 See this Slack history] for an example of how this materializes in #core.

summary: wp_update_term() reports success when the database write is rejected
_description:
`wp_update_term()` discards the return value of all three of its `$wpdb->update()` calls (`wp-includes/taxonomy.php:3418`, `:3422`, `:3450`). When a write is refused, the function still fires `edited_terms` / `edited_term`, clears the term cache, and returns `array( 'term_id' => …, 'term_taxonomy_id' => … )` — indistinguishable from a real update.
`wp_insert_term()` has the same unchecked call at `:2640`.

== Mechanism ==

`wpdb::process_fields()` (`wp-includes/class-wpdb.php:2812`) runs `strip_invalid_text()`, normalises each value to fit its column, compares the result against the input, and returns `false` if anything changed. `$wpdb->update()` then returns `false` without sending a query, so this is not MySQL truncation and strict mode is not involved.

The failure is also unrecoverable after the fact: `wpdb::flush()` resets `last_error` (`wp-includes/class-wpdb.php:1927`) and `wp_update_term()` runs several more queries before returning, so `$wpdb->last_error` is already empty when the caller receives the success array.

== Reproducing ==

'''1. Ordinary input.''' `terms.name` is `varchar(200)` and neither `wp_insert_term()` nor
`wp_update_term()` checks its length. Reaching the limit does not require a 200-character name:
the default `pre_term_name` filters (`_wp_specialchars`, `wp-includes/default-filters.php:33`)
expand `&` to `&` after submission.

{{{#!php
<?php
$name = str_repeat( 'a', 150 ) . str_repeat( ' & ', 12 ); // 186 characters as typed

$t = wp_insert_term( 'Example', 'category' );
$r = wp_update_term( $t['term_id'], 'category', array( 'name' => $name ) );

var_dump( $r );                              // array( 'term_id' => …, 'term_taxonomy_id' => … )
var_dump( get_term( $t['term_id'] )->name ); // "Example" — unchanged
}}}

'''2. Without any length involved.''' Any value `process_fields()` rejects behaves the same, so
a filter is enough:

{{{#!php
<?php
add_filter( 'wp_update_term_data', function ( $data ) {
      $data['name'] = "Bad\xED\xA0\x80name";   // 19 characters, invalid UTF-8 seque
      return $data;
} );
// wp_update_term() returns the success array; the row is unchanged.
}}}

== Both public write paths report success ==

* '''REST''' — `POST /wp/v2/categories/<id>` with the 186-character name returns '''200 OK''',
  the response body carries the '''old''' name, and the row is unchanged. The terms controller
  sets no `maxLength` on `name`.
* '''Admin''' — `wp-admin/edit-tags.php:183-186` treats the truthy, non-`WP_Error` return as
  success and redirects with `message=3`, "Item updated."

== Asymmetry with the insert path ==

`wp_insert_term()` checks both of its `$wpdb->insert()` calls (`:2628`, `:2656`) and returns `WP_Error( 'db_insert_error' )` for the same input, so create and update disagree on identical data.

== Related ==

* #36610 — over-length term ''names''; the input-validation half. A length guard belongs there.
* #46010, #31665 — the term ''slug'' side of the same 200-character column.

For reference, the Core Handbook has a [https://make.wordpress.org/core/handbook/tutorials/upgrading-node-js-npm-in-wordpress/ page documenting the related considerations and changes required when updating Node.js for WordPress] and includes a checklist to follow.

Some key dates:
- 20.x reached end-of-life on April 30, 2026.
- 22.x reaches EOL on April 30, 2027
- 24.x transitions to maintenance LTS on April 30, 2027.
- 26.x is Current and transitions to Active LTS in October 2026.
- Starting with version 27, the Node.js project is transitioning from an even/odd versioning practice (even releases only reach LTS status, odd releases are not meant for production use and supported only for 6 months) to an annual one (every release reaches LTS status after a 6 month Current phase).

Previously:
- #59663 - Node.js 20.x (18.x was skipped)
- #56658 - Node.js 16.x (#59187 for bundled themes)
- #52341 - Node.js 14.x (all older branches receiving security updates)
- #45241 - Node.js 10.x

summary: Block Bindings: Add innerBlock bindings compatibility.
_description:
Block bindings can currently only replace block attributes. This ticket proposes letting a block bindings source supply the inner blocks of a Group or Column block, through a new `innerBlocks` binding: {{{
}}} The source returns serialized block markup. The supplied blocks replace the block's own inner blocks before they render, with the block's context. An empty string leaves the block empty. Any other value, such as plain text, keeps the block's own inner blocks. How it works: * `WP_Block::process_block_bindings()` handles `innerBlocks` itself instead of treating it as an attribute. * The markup is sanitized with `wp_kses_post()`, as bound rich text already is, and custom CSS is removed from the supplied blocks. * Supplied blocks can't bind their own inner blocks, so two sources can't expand each other forever. * The blocks go where the block's own inner blocks were. A block without any gets them before the closing tag of its wrapper, found with the HTML API. * The editor isn't offered `innerBlocks` yet, as it doesn't render these bindings. Gutenberg PR: https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/85568

summary: wp_insert_user() allows duplicate email addresses containing an apostrophe
_description:
== Description ==

`wp_insert_user()` runs `pre_user_email`, which includes `wp_filter_kses`. That filter expects slashed input and returns slashed output, so for `o'brien@example.com` the value of `$user_email` at the duplicate check is `o\'brien@example.com`.

`email_exists( $user_email )` then queries for the literal backslashed string, never matches the stored row, and the duplicate check silently passes. The value is unslashed later via `wp_unslash( $compacted )`, so the duplicate is saved with the correct address.

[57711] (#52529) fixed the related comparison on update by slashing `$old_user_data->user_email`, but the `email_exists()` lookup was not changed.

== Steps to reproduce ==

Tested on trunk 7.2-alpha-63166, MariaDB 10.11.

{{{
wp_insert_user( wp_slash( array( 'user_login' => 'a', 'user_pass' => 'x', 'user_email' => "o'brien@example.com" ) ) );
wp_insert_user( wp_slash( array( 'user_login' => 'b', 'user_pass' => 'x', 'user_email' => "o'brien@example.com" ) ) );
// Second call succeeds. With plain@example.com it correctly returns existing_user_email.
}}}

Results with an existing user at `o'brien@example.com`:

||= Path =||= Result =||
|| `wp_insert_user()`, slashed input || duplicate created ||
|| `wp_insert_user()`, unslashed input || duplicate created ||
|| `wp_update_user()` moving another user to that email || allowed ||
|| `POST /wp/v2/users` (admin) || 201, duplicate created ||
|| `register_new_user()` || blocked (own `email_exists()` check) ||
|| `POST /wp/v2/users/me` (subscriber) || blocked (`rest_user_invalid_email`) ||

Front-end registration and self-service profile edits are protected by their own checks, so this needs `create_users` or direct API use. It is a data integrity issue, not a privilege escalation.

== Impact ==

Once duplicates exist, `get_user_by( 'email' )` returns whichever row the database hands back first. Anything keyed on email (password reset by email, login with email, plugins that look users up by email) can then resolve to the wrong account.

== Proposed fix ==

Run the comparison and lookup against the unslashed value, for example `$check_email = wp_unslash( $user_email );` used in both `strcasecmp()` and `email_exists()`. This could also make the slashing of `$old_user_data->user_email` from [57711] unnecessary, which is worth confirming in review.

Tests should cover insert (slashed and unslashed), update to another user's apostrophe email, and REST create, alongside the existing `test_reset_password_with_apostrophe_in_email()`.

summary: Plugin Dependencies: Undefined array key "activateUrl" for active plugins on multisite
Media endpoint returns 500 when an upload is rejected for a client reason
_description:
When `wp_handle_upload()` or `wp_handle_sideload()` rejects a file, `WP_REST_Attachments_Controller` returns status 500 whatever the reason:

 * `upload_from_file()`: `rest_upload_unknown_error`, 500
 * `upload_from_data()`: `rest_upload_sideload_error`, 500

Most of these rejections are caused by the request, not the server:

 * a file type the site does not allow,
 * an empty or partial file,
 * a file over `upload_max_filesize`,
 * a file a plugin rejected in `wp_handle_upload_prefilter` (size, dimension and naming policy plugins do this).

Other request checks in the same controller already return 400 (`rest_upload_no_data`, the multisite checks in `check_upload_size()`). The URL sideload path added in 7.2 also returns 400 for a disallowed type, by comparing the translated message string.

'''Why this matters more in 7.2:''' since [64588], uploads from the Media Library grid, Add New Media File and the media modal go through `POST /wp/v2/media` instead of `async-upload.php`. So every upload a plugin refuses, and every disallowed type, now shows up as an HTTP 500:

 * in server access logs,
 * in APM and uptime error rates,
 * in the browser console ("Failed to load resource: the server responded with a status of 500").

On 7.1 the same refusal from `async-upload.php` was a 200 with an error message.

=== Steps to reproduce (7.2-beta1-64675) ===

 1. Add this mu-plugin:
{{{#!php
<?php
add_filter( 'wp_handle_upload_prefilter', function ( $file ) {
	if ( false !== strpos( $file['name'], 'reject' ) ) {
		$file['error'] = 'Rejected by a plugin.';
	}
	return $file;
} );
}}}
 2. Go to Media > Add New Media File and upload `reject-me.jpg`. The UI shows "Rejected by a plugin.", but the request returns 500.

The same with an application password and curl:

||= Upload =||= Before =||= After =||
|| valid JPEG || 201 || 201 ||
|| `reject-me.jpg` (prefilter), multipart || 500 || 400 ||
|| `vector.svg` (type not allowed), multipart || 500 || 400 ||
|| `shell.php` (type not allowed), multipart || 500 || 400 ||
|| empty file, multipart || 500 || 400 ||
|| `reject-me.jpg`, raw body (sideload) || 500 || 400 ||
|| `vector.svg`, raw body (sideload) || 500 || 400 ||

Error codes and messages stay the same; only the status changes.

=== Patch ===

The controller cannot tell the reasons apart today: every failure reaches it as `array( 'error' => $message )`. The patch:

 1. `_wp_handle_upload()` passes an error code as a third argument to the upload error handler. The default `wp_handle_upload_error()` returns it as `error_code`. The codes:
   * `upload_prefilter_error`
   * `upload_invalid_form`
   * `upload_err_ini_size`, `upload_err_form_size`, `upload_err_partial`, `upload_err_no_file`, `upload_err_no_tmp_dir`, `upload_err_cant_write`, `upload_err_extension`, `upload_php_error`
   * `upload_failed_test`
   * `upload_empty_file`
   * `upload_invalid_file_type`
   * `upload_dir_error`
   * `upload_move_failed`
 2. A new `WP_REST_Attachments_Controller::get_upload_error_status()` returns 400 for the client errors and 500 for everything else, including no tmp dir, can't write, an uploads directory that can't be created, a file that can't be moved, and any error without a code.
 3. The URL sideload path checks `upload_invalid_file_type` instead of comparing the translated message.

=== Backward compatibility ===

 * The `error` key and every REST error code are unchanged. `error_code` is a new, optional key.
 * A custom `upload_error_handler` now receives a third argument. Userland functions ignore extra arguments. Only an internal PHP function used as the handler with a fixed argument count would complain, which seems unlikely.
 * A plugin that defines its own `wp_handle_upload_error()` before core does returns no `error_code`, so its errors keep the 500 status. Nothing changes for it.
 * Clients that treat 5xx as "retry" will no longer retry rejected uploads, which is the point. The media upload queue in `@wordpress/upload-media` decides retries from the error message, not the status, so it is unaffected. The Media Library chooses its text from the error code and message, so the UI is unchanged.

=== Open questions ===

 * Should the size errors (`upload_err_ini_size`, `upload_err_form_size`) be 413 instead of 400?
 * Should the type error use `rest_upload_invalid_file_type` everywhere, like the URL sideload path? I left the codes alone to keep the change small.

=== Tests ===

 * REST: a prefilter rejection, a disallowed type and a raw-body prefilter rejection return 400. An uploads directory that can't be created and a destination that can't be written return 500.
 * `wp_handle_sideload()` returns the right `error_code` for prefilter, empty file, type, uploads dir and move failures.
 * Eight of the ten new tests fail without the change. The two 500 tests guard the existing behavior.
 * `WP_Test_REST_Attachments_Controller`, `Tests_Admin_IncludesFile`, `Tests_Media` and `Tests_File`: 966 tests pass. The 20 warnings come from `Tests_Filesystem_WpOpcacheInvalidateDirectory` and are the same on trunk.
 * phpcs and PHPStan are clean on the changed files.

Use of AI tools: I used Claude Code to write the patch and tests, and draft this ticket. I reviewed the code and ran the tests and the reproduction myself.

summary: WP_Filesystem_SSH2 should verify the server's host key
_description:
`WP_Filesystem_SSH2::connect()` opens the connection with `ssh2_connect()` and then authenticates, without checking the server's host key. The `hostkey` option passed to `ssh2_connect()` only sets which key algorithms are accepted. It doesn't pin a key.

The PHP manual for `ssh2_connect()` recommends checking the key with `ssh2_fingerprint()` after connecting.

Possible approaches:

- Accept an expected fingerprint, through a constant such as `FTP_HOST_FINGERPRINT` or a field in the connection form. Compare it with `ssh2_fingerprint()` before authenticating, and refuse the connection if they don't match.
- Store the fingerprint the first time the site connects and refuse later connections if it changes, like OpenSSH's `known_hosts`.

Props lboy for the original report on HackerOne.

REST batch requests can pass WP_Error to rest_post_dispatch, causing TypeError
_description:
WordPress 7.1.3 can produce an HTTP 500 response when a REST API batch subrequest is short-circuited by a rest_pre_dispatch filter returning a WP_Error.

The REST batch handler in WP_REST_Server::serve_batch_request_v1() does not appear to normalize this error into a WP_REST_Response before invoking rest_post_dispatch.

Because rest_ensure_response() intentionally preserves WP_Error objects, callbacks expecting a REST response can receive an unexpected object type and trigger a PHP TypeError.

This appears to be a batch-processing equivalent of the issue previously addressed in #56566.

== Environment ==

* WordPress: 7.1.3
* PHP: 8.2.34 and 8.2.35
* Web server: Apache 2.4 with PHP-FPM
* Operating system: Debian 12

== Actual Behavior ==

Production logs recorded the following fatal error:

{{{
PHP Fatal error: Uncaught TypeError:
_wp_connectors_rest_settings_dispatch():
Argument #1 ($response) must be of type WP_REST_Response,
WP_Error given

wp-includes/connectors.php:697
}}}

The stack trace includes:

{{{
WP_REST_Server->serve_batch_request_v1()
WP_REST_Server->respond_to_request()
WP_REST_Server->dispatch()
}}}

The error occurred three times on October 13, 2026, and three additional times on October 25, 2026.

Each occurrence corresponded closely to an HTTP 500 response.

The issue was observed before and after upgrading PHP from 8.2.34 to 8.2.35.

== Root Cause Analysis ==

Source inspection indicates that serve_batch_request_v1() handles rest_pre_dispatch results differently from the normal REST dispatch path.

When a rest_pre_dispatch filter returns a WP_Error, the batch handler can bypass normal dispatch processing.

The batch handler subsequently executes logic equivalent to:

{{{
$result = rest_ensure_response( $result );

$result = apply_filters(
‘rest_post_dispatch’,
$result,
$this,
$single_request
);
}}}

However, rest_ensure_response() returns WP_Error objects unchanged.

Consequently, rest_post_dispatch can receive a WP_Error rather than the expected response object.

In WordPress 7.1.3, _wp_connectors_rest_settings_dispatch() requires a WP_REST_Response, producing the observed fatal error.

== Expected Behavior ==

When a REST batch subrequest returns a WP_Error through rest_pre_dispatch, WordPress should normalize that error into an appropriate REST response before invoking rest_post_dispatch.

For example, a batch subrequest producing a WP_Error with HTTP status 403 should result in:

* An outer batch response with HTTP status 207.
* A nested subrequest response with HTTP status 403.
* The original REST error code and message preserved.
* No PHP fatal error.

== Suggested Fix ==

Normalize WP_Error objects before applying rest_post_dispatch within serve_batch_request_v1().

For example:

{{{
$result = rest_ensure_response( $result );

if ( is_wp_error( $result ) ) {
$result = $this->error_to_response( $result );
}

$result = apply_filters(
‘rest_post_dispatch’,
$result,
$this,
$single_request
);
}}}

This would align the batch handler with the error normalization already implemented in the normal REST dispatch path.

The proposed correction is based on source inspection and has not yet been validated by automated tests.

== Suggested Regression Test ==

A PHPUnit test could:

1. Register a valid REST route supporting batch requests.
2. Add a rest_pre_dispatch filter returning a 403 WP_Error for that route.
3. Dispatch a request through /batch/v1.
4. Assert that the outer response returns HTTP 207.
5. Assert that the nested response returns HTTP 403 with the expected error code.
6. Verify that rest_post_dispatch receives a valid response object.

Source inspection suggests that a valid batch subrequest can trigger this condition when a rest_pre_dispatch filter returns WP_Error. This has not yet been independently verified with a regression test.

== Related Tickets ==

‘’’#56566 — Fatal error when WP_REST_Server::dispatch() returns WP_Error’’’

https://core.trac.wordpress.org/ticket/56566

This ticket corrected a similar error-normalization problem in the normal REST dispatch path. The batch handler appears to have an equivalent unhandled path.

‘’’#66136 — REST batch request handling issue’’’

https://core.trac.wordpress.org/ticket/66136

This concerns malformed batch subrequest paths and appears distinct from the error-normalization issue described here.

== Testing Status ==

The issue has been observed repeatedly in production logs, and the relevant WordPress source code has been inspected.

A standalone PHPUnit reproduction has not yet been executed.

The identity of the rest_pre_dispatch callback responsible for producing the original WP_Error in production has not been established.

No WordPress core files were modified on the affected installation.

This report is being submitted to document the failure and proposed correction for further investigation and testing by WordPress core contributors.
