summary: KSES: Re-implement using HTML API
_description:
Since its initial commit, WordPress has relied on the KSES library to sanitize and normalize and transform content from untrusted sources. Unfortunately, the parsing inside of `wp_kses()` has never been spec-compliant, leading to numerous challenges in safely, efficiently, and reliably fulfilling its purpose.

The HTML API provides a mechanism for structurally interacting with HTML in an efficient manner, and `wp_kses()` should be rewritten to lean on that existing capability.

== Resolves

 - #25851 Large attribute values may crash PCRE patterns and cause content loss.
 - #37698 Global pollution in `wp_kses_split()` calls.
 - #48873 CSS contents are corrupted by `wp_kses()`.
 - #51482 `wp_kses()` turns SCRIPT and STYLE content into renderable text.
 - #52333 `wp_kses()` and HTML disagree on the set of named character references.
 - #58377 Block names with consecutive hyphens are corrupted.
 - #58921 Valid tag names are rejected from the allow-list.
 - #59310 `parse_blocks()` called unnecessarily.
 - #61246 `wp_kses()` un-comments HTML comments.
 - #62024 `wp_kses_post()` incorrectly escapes “<” in attribute values.

=== Potentially resolves

 - #51093 CSS `>` corruption.
 - #56118 Slashes are improperly stripped when exporting data.

== Related

 - #63881 Deprecate `wp_kses_stripslashes()`.
 - #65599 HTML sanitization API implementation.

summary: MCP setup on the Connectors screen
_description:
== Problem ==

Settings → Connectors is WordPress's central place for setting up integrations and even promotes AI experiments and third-party proprietary AI connectors (with no inherent functionality). 

The official MCP Adapter is now available in the WordPress.org plugin directory, but a site owner who wants to connect an MCP client still has to discover the adapter, find the correct endpoint for their site, create an Application Password, and translate those details into a client-specific configuration. Activating the plugin does not currently provide that path on the Connectors screen.

This is a different task from choosing which WordPress abilities are exposed over MCP. The proposed card helps a person connect a client to their own site; exposure controls can remain with the adapter or another dedicated interface.

== Proposal ==

Add a first-party "WordPress MCP" card to Settings → Connectors. The card would guide an authorized user through:

 1. Installing and activating the official MCP Adapter (`mcp-adapter`) from the WordPress.org plugin directory through an explicit "Install and activate" action when it is missing, or an "Activate" action when it is installed but inactive. Use Core's existing Plugins REST API and normal installation and activation permissions. Show a useful explanation when installation is unavailable (for example, file modifications are disabled).
 2. Showing the site's actual MCP endpoint and whether Application Passwords are available for the current user. Resolve the endpoint from the active adapter/server registration so subdirectory installs and plain permalinks work.
 3. Choosing an MCP client and creating a separately named, revocable Application Password for that client through WordPress's existing API, only after the user requests it. Provide a copyable configuration for supported clients and a link to revoke the credential from the user's profile. (This part is debatable, perhaps it's just a link to the plugin documentation which can be updated more frequently.)
 4. Explaining what to do next, including a first test to run in the selected client and the "connected but no abilities available" state. Link to the adapter's documentation or diagnostics where appropriate.

The card should use the existing Connectors UI and WordPress design-system components. It should distinguish "adapter installed" and "ready to connect" from a verified client connection; merely showing an endpoint is not proof that a client has connected.

Application Passwords inherit the permissions of the WordPress account that creates them. The setup flow should make that clear, show the generated secret only at creation, and avoid storing it in connector settings or exposing it in subsequent page loads. If Application Passwords are unavailable, the card should explain the reason where WordPress can determine it and provide an actionable next step.

== Why in Core? ==

Core owns the Connectors screen and already provides a path for discovering and installing connector plugins. A guide supplied only by MCP Adapter or AI Experiments cannot appear before the plugin is installed, which leaves the first step undiscoverable. A first-party MCP card would make the site-to-client setup available in the same place before and after installation. The MCP server would still come from the optional MCP Adapter plugin; this proposal does not add an MCP server to Core. It also allows plugins to remove their own custom MCP setup instructions and settings pages and centralize on one UI entry point.

The working prototype below demonstrates the flow on the Connectors screen. It registers a non-credential connector and adds a custom card, but relies on experimental @wordpress/connectors JavaScript exports. Core can use the prototype to test the interaction while settling the final ownership of client configuration templates and adapter status data.

Prototype: https://github.com/bacoords/mcp-connection-guide
Live WordPress Playground demo: https://playground.wordpress.net/?blueprint-url=https%3A%2F%2Fraw.githubusercontent.com%2Fbacoords%2Fmcp-connection-guide%2Fmain%2Fblueprint.json
Screenshots: https://github.com/bacoords/mcp-connection-guide/tree/main/docs/screenshots

== Suggested acceptance criteria ==

 * The card is discoverable on Settings → Connectors and can install/activate the official MCP Adapter from the plugin directory when the user has the required capabilities. No plugin installation occurs merely from viewing the page.
 * Missing adapter, inactive adapter, failed installation, disabled file modifications, unavailable Application Passwords, and insufficient permissions each have a clear state and next step.
 * The endpoint is derived from the registered MCP server and works for subdirectory installs and plain permalinks.
 * Creating a credential requires an explicit action. A separate Application Password can be named for each client; its value is shown once, is not saved in Connector settings, and has a clear revocation path.
 * Generated setup instructions use the active site's endpoint and supported authentication method. They are accessible, keyboard-operable, localizable, and built with existing WordPress UI components.
 * A site with no abilities exposed over MCP has an understandable explanation rather than appearing silently broken.

== Related work ==

 * Connectors custom-card extensibility: #64791
 * MCP Adapter in the plugin directory: https://wordpress.org/plugins/mcp-adapter/
 * MCP Adapter site-owner onboarding discussion: https://github.com/WordPress/mcp-adapter/issues/369
 * MCP Adapter Site Health diagnostics proposal: https://github.com/WordPress/mcp-adapter/pull/376
 * AI plugin MCP Access proposal, focused on ability exposure: https://github.com/WordPress/ai/pull/992
 * Earlier AI plugin MCP admin UI and client-configuration exploration (closed without merging): https://github.com/WordPress/ai/pull/152

Two profiles appear, and they need different fixes. `Tests_WpTokenMap` and `Tests_Canonical_PostStatus` are data-provider matrices of cheap tests, so the lever is the size of the matrix. `Tests_Admin_ExportWp` and `Tests_Image_Editor_Imagick` are a few expensive tests, so the lever is fixture and I/O cost inside each one.

== How to work a class ==

 1. Claim it in a comment here, one class at a time.
 2. Measure before: `npm run test:php -- --filter Class_Name`, then read the `time` attributes in `tests/phpunit/build/logs/junit.xml`.
 3. Apply the levers the handbook already documents: hoist immutable fixtures into `wpSetUpBeforeClass()`, share expensive objects across the class, trim provider matrices that exercise identical code paths, and mock file or image work where the assertion does not need the real thing.
 4. Measure after, the same way, and post both numbers on this ticket with the PR.

Guardrails: no assertion is removed to save time, no expected value changes to make a test pass, no timeouts are raised, and a test that protects a specific behavior stays even if it is slow.

Related: #42904, #42278 and #41451 (older performance proposals that can now be evaluated against data), #63026 (the bcrypt precedent), #52645, #65887.

Introduce constant or filter to prevent wp-cron.php triggering cron jobs.
_description:
The constant `DISABLE_WP_CRON` allows developers to [https://developer.wordpress.org/apis/wp-config-php/#disable-cron-and-cron-timeout prevent the triggering of loopback requests] to the `wp-cron.php` endpoint.

However, the constant does not prevent the `wp-cron.php` endpoint from running events registered via the WP Cron API.

`DISABLE_WP_CRON` was introduced prior to the existence of WP-CLI, so the recommended method for executing jobs via real cron was to execute the script directly or use curl to call the endpoint.

Now that WP CLI does exist, the best method for running wp-cron via real cron is to call `wp cron event run --due-now` or similar.

With this new best practice, I think it would be beneficial to allow developers to disable the wp-cron.php endpoint. Hitting the endpoint can be resource intensive and, for sites using real cron, lead to conflicts.

I think a constant or filter `disable_wp_cron_endpoint` would be beneficial in the context of modern sites using WP CLI.

The value of `DISABLE_WP_CRON` would need to default to the new filter/constant as firing loopback requests to an endpoint that doesn't do anything would be a little bit silly.

summary: Parse content for shortcodes instead of using regex
_description:
Shortcodes are currently "parsed" out of content using a regular expression and a call to `preg_replace_callback()`. This causes some issues like the inability to use a square bracket in a shortcode attribute.

I've written and attached to this ticket a lexer/parser that steps through the content character by character, finding shortcodes and calling `do_shortcode_tag()` for each one as soon as it's completely parsed.  It passes every existing shortcode unit test, as well as six additional tests I've added. It fixes tickets #49955 and #43725 and may possibly fix others that deal with shortcode edge cases.

This method has the advantage of being able to deal with content that wouldn't be properly extracted by a regular expression. Take this string for example:

{{{
[shortcode1][shortcode2 att="[/shortcode1]" /][/shortcode1]
}}}

The current implementation would parse this as a single shortcode:

* `[shortcode1]` with inner content `[shortcode2 att="`

The parse I've attached properly recognizes it as two shortcodes:

* `[shortcode1]` with inner content `[shortcode2 att="[/shortcode1]" /]`
* `[shortcode2]` with attribute `att="[/shortcode1]"`

summary: Check for a non-string _method parameter in WP_REST_Server::serve_request()
_description:
`WP_REST_Server::serve_request()` lets the `_method` query parameter override the request method. It only checks that `_method` is set ( [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/trunk/src/wp-includes/rest-api/class-wp-rest-server.php#L438-L439 GH] ) and then passes it to `WP_REST_Request::set_method()`, which calls `strtoupper()` on it ( [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/trunk/src/wp-includes/rest-api/class-wp-rest-request.php#L206 GH] ). A string like `?_method=POST` works fine, but `?_method[]=POST` makes it an array. This happens before routing, so any REST API URL can reach it. You can easily create a PHP fatal error by sending an array: {{{ $ curl -g -i 'localhost:8889/wp-json/?_method[]=POST' HTTP/1.1 200 OK Server: nginx/1.29.7 Date: Mon, 26 Oct 2026 21:14:49 GMT Content-Type: application/json; charset=UTF-8 Transfer-Encoding: chunked Connection: keep-alive X-Powered-By: PHP/8.3.30 X-Robots-Tag: noindex Link: ; rel="https://api.w.org/" X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
Fatal error: Uncaught TypeError: strtoupper(): Argument #1 ($string) must be of type string, array given in /var/www/src/wp-includes/rest-api/class-wp-rest-request.php:206 Stack trace: #0 /var/www/src/wp-includes/rest-api/class-wp-rest-request.php(206): strtoupper(Array) #1 /var/www/src/wp-includes/rest-api/class-wp-rest-server.php(439): WP_REST_Request->set_method(Array) #2 /var/www/src/wp-includes/rest-api.php(496): WP_REST_Server->serve_request('/') #3 /var/www/src/wp-includes/class-wp-hook.php(369): rest_api_loaded(Object(WP)) #4 /var/www/src/wp-includes/class-wp-hook.php(393): WP_Hook->apply_filters('', Array) #5 /var/www/src/wp-includes/plugin.php(582): WP_Hook->do_action(Array) #6 /var/www/src/wp-includes/class-wp.php(417): do_action_ref_array('parse_request', Array) #7 /var/www/src/wp-includes/class-wp.php(877): WP->parse_request('') #8 /var/www/src/wp-includes/functions.php(1375): WP->main('') #9 /var/www/src/wp-blog-header.php(16): wp() #10 /var/www/src/_index.php(17): require('/var/www/src/wp...') #11 /var/www/src/index.php(19): require_once('/var/www/src/_i...') #12 {main} thrown in /var/www/src/wp-includes/rest-api/class-wp-rest-request.php on line 206
}}} WordPress needs to check that `_method` is a string before using it to override the request method. Instead of a `HTTP 200` the response should be `400 Bad Request` with JSON data indicating it what the error is. I have a PR to address this.

summary: Name the item, or give a count, in the plugin/theme auto-update email subject lines
_description:
Follow-up of #50268, where the current subject lines were introduced in 5.5.

The subject line of the plugin/theme auto-update email is the same regardless of how many items were updated, and never says which ones. Plugins release independently of one another, so a run that has anything to do usually has a single plugin to do it for. Among the 100 most popular plugins in the directory, the median gap between releases is around 50 days, and their most recent releases fall on 40 different days. The update check runs twice a day. So the site admin sees, over and over:

{{{
[My Site] Some plugins were automatically updated
}}}

for a body that reads:

{{{
These plugins are now up to date:
- Jetpack (from version 16.1.2 to 16.1.3) : https://wordpress.org/plugins/jetpack/
}}}

The subject carries none of the information the admin actually wants, so every one of these emails has to be opened before it can be triaged or filed. Someone running a handful of sites receives a stream of identical subjects and has no way to tell, from the inbox, which one is worth a look.

== Proposal ==

When a single item of a single type was updated, name it in the subject. Otherwise, give a count instead of the word "Some".

So the two most common emails become:

{{{
[My Site] Jetpack was automatically updated
[My Site] 3 plugins were automatically updated
}}}

Plugin and theme names are not bounded in length, and some run well past what a mail client shows. A name that long should be truncated before it goes in the subject, around 40 characters with an ellipsis.

'''Success emails''' (subject built from `$successful_updates`):

|| '''Case''' || '''Current''' || '''Proposed''' ||
|| 1 plugin || `[%s] Some plugins were automatically updated` || `[%1$s] %2$s was automatically updated` ||
|| N plugins || `[%s] Some plugins were automatically updated` || `[%1$s] %2$d plugins were automatically updated` ||
|| 1 theme || `[%s] Some themes were automatically updated` || `[%1$s] %2$s was automatically updated` ||
|| N themes || `[%s] Some themes were automatically updated` || `[%1$s] %2$d themes were automatically updated` ||
|| plugins + themes || `[%s] Some plugins and themes have automatically updated` || `[%1$s] %2$d plugins and %3$d themes were automatically updated` ||

'''Failure and mixed emails''' (subject built from `$failed_updates`, as it is today):

|| '''Case''' || '''Current''' || '''Proposed''' ||
|| 1 plugin || `[%s] Some plugins have failed to update` || `[%1$s] %2$s failed to update` ||
|| N plugins || `[%s] Some plugins have failed to update` || `[%1$s] %2$d plugins have failed to update` ||
|| 1 theme || `[%s] Some themes have failed to update` || `[%1$s] %2$s failed to update` ||
|| N themes || `[%s] Some themes have failed to update` || `[%1$s] %2$d themes have failed to update` ||
|| plugins + themes || `[%s] Some plugins and themes have failed to update` || `[%1$s] %2$d plugins and %3$d themes have failed to update` ||

The email body is unchanged in every case.

Sites can already do all of this through the `auto_plugin_theme_update_email` filter, but the default is what the great majority of admins actually receive, and the information is right there when the subject is built.

Related: #50268, #50350, #51695, #53049

summary: Application password UX improvements
_description:
This ticket covers several related UX improvements for the application password approval screen.

These apply to the screen at `wp-admin/authorize-application.php` and its various URL query parameters.

1. Increase clarity about the target URL that will receive credentials if the request is approved. The only aspect of this URL that the user should be concerned about is its host name, and it should be front and centre.
2. Remove support for `username:password@` credentials in URLs. These are deprecated in modern browsers and used almost exclusively for phishing.
3. Remove support for a reject URL. If a user rejects a request, a reject URL allows the user to still be phished.
4. Add a "Copy" button to the generated application password after approval.

I've been working on these enhancements in https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/11079.

Any further suggested improvements should go into separate tickets.

Tests: Add PHPUnit tests for wp_json_encode(
_description:
The `wp_json_encode()` function in `wp-includes/functions.php` is a wrapper around `json_encode()` that provides additional logic, such as handling UTF-8 encoding issues and applying the `wp_php_error_args` filter.

This patch introduces a new test class `Tests_Functions_WpGetUpdatePhpUrl` to provide coverage for:
- The default URL return value.
- Overriding the URL via the `WP_UPDATE_PHP_URL` environment variable.
- Overriding the URL via the `wp_update_php_url` filter.

summary: Tests: Add PHPUnit tests for get_dirsize()
_description:
The `get_dirsize()` function in `wp-includes/functions.php` calculates the total size of a directory in bytes. It relies on `recurse_dirsize()` to perform the actual calculation and supports features like excluding specific subdirectories and enforcing a maximum execution time.

Currently, this function lacks dedicated unit test coverage in the core suite. This patch introduces a new test class `Tests_Functions_GetDirsize` to verify:
- Accurate size calculation for directories containing files and subdirectories.
- Proper handling of the `$exclude` parameter.
- Correct behaviour for non-existent or unreadable directories.
- Support for the `pre_recurse_dirsize` filter to short-circuit calculation.
- Basic verification of the transient-based caching mechanism (`dirsize_cache`).

summary: Tests: Add PHPUnit tests for wp_die() and its handlers
_description:
The `wp_die()` function in `wp-includes/functions.php` is the standard way to terminate WordPress execution with an error message. It supports multiple handlers based on the request type (Ajax, JSON, XML-RPC, REST, etc.) and allows for custom handlers via filters.

Currently, while `wp_die()` is used extensively throughout the test suite, it lacks dedicated unit tests to verify its core logic and the behavior of its default handlers:
- `_default_wp_die_handler()`
- `_ajax_wp_die_handler()`
- `_json_wp_die_handler()`
- `_jsonp_wp_die_handler()`
- `_xml_wp_die_handler()`
- `_xmlrpc_wp_die_handler()`

This patch introduces a new test class `Tests_Functions_wpDie` (and potentially separate files for handlers following the `@covers` rule) to verify:
- Correct handler selection based on request context.
- Argument parsing and sanitization via `_wp_die_process_input()`.
- Proper output formatting for different handlers (HTML, JSON, XML).
- Respecting the `exit` argument to prevent process termination during testing.
- Application of various `wp_die_{type}_handler` filters.

summary: KSES: Allow CSS color functions in inline styles
_description:
Backport of Gutenberg PR https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/84213.

safecss_filter_attr() drops any declaration whose value uses a CSS color function, such as rgb(), hsl(), oklch() or color-mix(). So box-shadow: 1px 1px 1px rgba(0,0,0,0.5) never reaches the page. The same goes for a shadow or text color from the style engine.

It removes a color function from the test string, innermost first, only when its contents are plain color syntax. Anything left over, such as a parenthesis, backslash, comment or unknown function, is still rejected. The check runs before the safecss_filter_attr_allow_css filter, so a plugin can still reject the declaration.

summary: Use the semantic HTML <search> element in core search markup
_description:
== Summary == The HTML [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/search ] element is now part of [https://web.dev/baseline Baseline] and is supported in all evergreen browsers (Chrome 118+, Firefox 118+, Safari 17+, Edge 118+). It is a semantic landmark element that represents a group of search/filtering controls and has an implicit ARIA role of search. WordPress currently produces search markup by adding `role="search"` to the surrounding `
` in several places: - `get_search_form()` in `wp-includes/general-template.php` (both the `html5` and `xhtml` formats). - The `core/search` block render callback in `wp-includes/blocks/search.php`. - Bundled classic themes that override `searchform.php` (Twenty Sixteen, Twenty Seventeen, Twenty Twenty, Twenty Twenty-One). This ticket proposes updating core search markup and bundled themes to use the native `` element, which removes the need for the explicit `role="search"` attribute and brings WordPress in line with current HTML semantics. == Background == The `` element was added to the HTML Living Standard to provide a dedicated semantic container for search functionality, similar to how `
` covers navigation and `
` covers primary content. Per the HTML spec: > The search element represents a part of a document or application that contains a set of form controls or other content related to performing a search or filtering operation. Today, the equivalent semantics are conveyed by adding `role="search"` to the surrounding ``. With the new element widely available, the `role` attribute can be dropped in favor of native markup. == Current state in core == `wp-includes/general-template.php` (`get_search_form()`, `html5` format): {{{ }}} `wp-includes/blocks/search.php` (`render_block_core_search()`): {{{#!php return sprintf( '
%4s
', esc_url( home_url( '/' ) ), $wrapper_attributes, $form_directives, $label . $field_markup ); }}} Bundled themes with their own `searchform.php` follow the same `
` pattern: - `src/wp-content/themes/twentysixteen/searchform.php` - `src/wp-content/themes/twentyseventeen/searchform.php` - `src/wp-content/themes/twentytwenty/searchform.php` - `src/wp-content/themes/twentytwentyone/searchform.php` - Newer block themes (Twenty Twenty-Two through Twenty Twenty-Five) inherit markup from the `core/search` block and need no theme-level change. == Proposal == Wrap each search form in a `` element and drop the now-redundant `role="search"` attribute on the inner ``: {{{ }}} For `get_search_form()`, the optional `aria_label` argument moves from the `
` to the new `` landmark element, since the landmark is what assistive technology exposes. The `xhtml` fallback in `get_search_form()` is left unchanged because XHTML 1.x does not include the `` element. Why drop `role="search"`? Keeping it on the inner `` while the `` wrapper also carries the implicit search role would produce nested search landmarks, which assistive technology may announce twice or report as a structural error. The HTML spec's intent is that `` replaces the manual role. == Patch == Patch and full test plan in the linked GitHub PR: [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/11913 wordpress-develop#11913] — General: Use the semantic `` element in core search markup Two atomic commits: General: `get_search_form()` (html5) + `core/search` block. Bundled Themes: Twenty Sixteen, Twenty Seventeen, Twenty Twenty, Twenty Twenty-One `searchform.php`. == Backward compatibility == - The `` element, its `class="search-form"`, and all input markup are unchanged. Theme CSS targeting `form.search-form` or `.wp-block-search` continues to work. - For the `core/search` block, block wrapper attributes (block class names, user-added classes) and Interactivity API directives remain on the `` to preserve block CSS, hydration boundaries, and event handling. - Browsers that pre-date `` support treat it as a generic inline container with no landmark role. Forms still function and remain accessible via the `` itself; the only loss is the explicit landmark announcement, which is no worse than the current state where `role="search"` is unsupported. - Custom themes that override `searchform.php` are unaffected; this change only touches core defaults and bundled classic themes. - The `get_search_form` and `search_form_format` filters continue to operate on the final HTML. == Accessibility == - `` has the implicit ARIA role search, replacing the manual `role="search"`. - Screen readers that already announce the search landmark will continue to do so via the native element on supporting UAs. - The `aria_label` argument now labels the `` landmark directly, which is the standard pattern for distinguishing multiple search landmarks on the same page. == Tasks == - Patch `get_search_form()` (`html5` format). - Patch `render_block_core_search()`. - Patch bundled classic themes (Sixteen, Seventeen, Twenty, Twenty-One). - Audit Twenty Twenty-Two through Twenty Twenty-Five for any inline search markup outside `core/search`. - Update unit and E2E tests if any assert on `role="search"` markup (initial scan found none). - Update developer documentation referencing ``. - Confirm screen reader behavior across VoiceOver, NVDA, JAWS, and TalkBack on the patched markup. == Open questions == - Should we keep an explicit `role="search"` attribute on the `` element for assistive technology that doesn't yet map `` to the search landmark role? It would be redundant for compliant UAs but defensive for older AT during a transition period. - Should the `core/search` block bump its `apiVersion` or expose a version flag so theme/block consumers can detect the markup change? - Should the `searchform.php` change also be backported to Twenty Sixteen / Seventeen, given their long support tail, or limited to Twenty Twenty and later? == References == MDN: [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/search HTML element] HTML spec: [https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/grouping-content.html#the-search-element 4.4.14 The search element] Baseline: [https://web.dev/baseline is widely available] GitHub PR: [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/11913 wordpress-develop#11913]

Toolbar: same W and site name behavior in the admin, the editors and the front end
_description:
This ticket proposes two fixed links in the Toolbar. The W always goes to the Dashboard. The site name always goes to the site. Both work the same in the admin, in the editors and on the front end.

It replaces #66235, which covered only the site name.

== Current behavior ==

The W and the site name are the first two items of the Toolbar.

 * A click on the W goes to the About WordPress page. It is the first item of the Toolbar, and it goes to a page people rarely need.
 * A click on the site name changes with the place. In the admin it goes to the site. On the front end it goes to the Dashboard.
 * The site name menu also changes. In the admin it has only Visit Site. On the front end it has Dashboard, Plugins and Themes.
 * When the site has no site icon, the icon changes too. It is a house in the admin and a gauge on the front end.

Since 7.1 the Toolbar is also displayed in the editors. There, the Toolbar has no link to the Dashboard. The W goes to the About page and the site name goes to the site.

== Proposal ==

'''The W'''

 * Click: the W always goes to the Dashboard.
 * Menu: Dashboard is the first item. The other items stay the same.
 * Small screens: the W stays visible. Today it is hidden under 600px.

[[Image(toolbar-w-menu.png)]]

'''The site name'''

 * Click: the site name always goes to the site.
 * Menu: the same items everywhere. Visit Site, Plugins and Themes. On multisite, Manage Site comes right after Visit Site.
 * Icon: the site icon when the site has one, as it works since 7.1. When the site has no site icon, the same default icon everywhere.

[[Image(toolbar-site-name-menu.png)]]

The Dashboard has one place, under the W. It leaves the site name menu.

Small screens:

[[Image(toolbar-small-screens.png)]]

== Why ==

 * The W gets a useful click. The logo in the top left corner is the most visible item of the Toolbar. I believe people expect it to go to the home of the admin. About WordPress is still in the menu, one click away.
 * The W menu keeps its role. It still holds the links about WordPress. Only the click changes.
 * One click to the Dashboard from everywhere. This matters most in the editors, where the Toolbar has no way back to the Dashboard today.
 * One behavior to learn. Each item does one thing. People don't need to check where they are before they click.
 * Two clear places. The W is the admin and the site name is the site. Today one item switches between both.
 * It works on multisite. My Sites stays next to the W, as today. In the Network Admin, the W goes to the network Dashboard.
 * **Better on touch screens**. A tap on the site name opens the menu. Today, in the admin, that menu has a single item.

== Accessibility ==

 * The accessible name of the W becomes "Dashboard". Today it is "About WordPress". The name says where the link goes.
 * Keyboard and focus behavior does not change.
 * Both menus have the same items in the same order everywhere. It is more predictable for screen reader users.
 * The site icon is decorative. The site name stays next to it.

== Backward compatibility ==

 * Two clicks change. The W goes to the Dashboard and not to the About page. On the front end, the site name goes to the site and not to the Dashboard.
 * The Dashboard item moves from the site name menu to the W menu. It keeps its ID.
 * People only see the items they have access to, same as today.
 * Classic themes keep their extra items (Widgets, Menus, Background and Header) after Themes.
 * The other menu items keep their IDs. Plugins that add items to these menus keep working.
 * Under 600px the Toolbar gets one more item, the W.

== Related ==

 * #66235 is the first version of this proposal, only for the site name. I will close it in favor of this ticket.
 * #28398 and #19184 asked for fixed links years ago and were closed. Since then, the site name got the site icon and the Toolbar is displayed in the editors.
 * #65088 site icon in the Toolbar.
 * #65091 Toolbar in the Site Editor and Block Editor.

Client-Side Media: Move `image_editor_output_format` filtering to the upload response
_description:
In [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/10868 #10868] (Editor: PHP backports for Client Side Media), the `image_editor_output_format` filter is currently applied in the REST API index (`get_index`) by iterating over a list of possible input MIME types with an empty `$output_formats` array and no `$filename` parameter. As noted in [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/10868#discussion_r2831587138 this review comment], this doesn't match how `wp_get_image_editor_output_format()` normally applies the filter — it passes the actual filename and a pre-populated default mapping.

== Problem ==

The current approach:
* Passes an empty array as the default value instead of the normal default mapping
* Does not supply a `$filename` parameter to the filter
* Re-filters the same `$output_formats` variable across iterations, accumulating results in a way that doesn't match the server-side behavior
* Is applied generically rather than per-upload, so plugins can't make decisions based on the actual input file

== Proposed Solution ==

Move the `image_editor_output_format` logic from the REST API index response into the '''initial image upload response'''. This is already the pattern used for EXIF rotation data in client-side media processing.

Benefits:
* The actual input filename and MIME type will be available, so the filter operates just like it does on the server side
* Plugins that hook into `image_editor_output_format` will receive meaningful parameters
* Keeps per-file processing logic in the upload response where it belongs

== References ==

* PR: [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/10868 #10868]
* Review: [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/10868#discussion_r2831587138 @westonruter's comment]
* Response: [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/10868#discussion_r2832131664 @adamsilverstein's response]

summary: set_transient() allows invalid transient name
_description:
Due to a typo/bug in my plugin code, I found that WordPress accepts empty strings, null, and false for the `$transient` arg, aka: the transient name, in `set_transient()` function which creates transients in the options database with values of simply `_transient_` and `_transient_timeout_`.

That said... the transient created with an empty string continued to work (could be set and get and deleted). Because the typo in my code referenced a variable that held the transient name but was empty, the get, set, and delete function calls worked (annoyingly).

I did observer two issues...

1. In the event two developers cause the same mistake/error, their transients will collide with each other.

2. More importantly, I observed the empty string transient will not be cleaned up by the delete_expired_transients routine. (The Transients Manager plugin must use delete_expired_transients() as it could not delete the transient either.) I will submit a second ticket for this issue.

Upon review of the set_transient() and add_option() code, I observed several opportunities to improve, including:

- return false for empty $transient value
- return false for bool, non-scalar $transient values
- cast $transient as string
- return false for strings with more than 172 characters

These false returns will guide developers to fix issues with malformed $transient names.

I have a pull request to github ready to follow this ticket.

summary: kses filter silently strips allowfullscreen from Vimeo and YouTube iframe embeds on every post save, breaking video playback sitewide
_description:
Every time a WordPress post containing a Vimeo or YouTube iframe embed is saved or updated, the kses filter silently strips the allowfullscreen attribute from the embed code in the database. This causes the embedded video to display a privacy/playback error to all visitors with no warning to the site owner — without my knowledge. I never know how long videos have not been working. This is not acceptable.

Steps to reproduce:

Embed a Vimeo or YouTube video in a post using the standard iframe embed code provided by those platforms
Save the post
Visit the post as a visitor — the video displays: “Because of its privacy settings, this video cannot be played here”
Inspect the post content in the database — allowfullscreen has been silently removed

Why this is a defect:

WordPress’s own embed block and oEmbed system generate iframe code that includes allowfullscreen. The kses filter then strips it on save — meaning WordPress is actively breaking its own output with zero warning to the user.

allowfullscreen is not a security risk. It is a standard HTML5 attribute that permits an iframe to enter fullscreen mode. It poses no cross-site scripting risk, no injection vector, and no security concern of any kind. It has been a standard part of the HTML5 specification since 2012.

Real-world impact:

I have operated a professional WordPress broadcast platform since 2009. Over nearly two decades, I have hosted leaders from every major industry — producing close to 300 episodes of long-form video interviews and 300 audio episodes that serve as a permanent public archive. This is serious, professional publishing work on WordPress.

This issue has been silently breaking professional video publishers like me for over a decade. A site with hundreds of video episodes can have every single video broken simultaneously simply because the site owner edited and saved a post for any reason — fixing a typo, updating metadata, adding a transcript. There is no warning. Visitors see broken videos. The site owner has no idea until a visitor reports it.

I want to be more active on my site — updating content, adding transcripts for accessibility and SEO, improving posts. But every time I save a post, my entire video library breaks. This is not a theoretical edge case. This is a recurring, documented failure that is actively discouraging professional publishers from maintaining and improving their WordPress sites.

My site is itsrainmakingtime.ch — a broadcast platform that has been live on WordPress since 2009.

Requested fix:

Add allowfullscreen to the kses allowed attributes whitelist for iframe elements. This is a one-line fix that would permanently resolve a user-hostile bug that has persisted since 2012.

I respectfully urge the WordPress core team to prioritize this fix. Professional publishers deserve better.

Thank you in advance. 

Kim Greenhouse
itsrainmakingtime.ch

REST API: rest_filter_response_fields() fatals on PHP 8 when response data is stdClass (e.g. /wp/v2/taxonomies?type=…&_fields=…)
_description:
On PHP 8+, requesting a taxonomy collection with _fields can fatal instead of returning a trimmed JSON response.

rest_filter_response_fields() passes response data into _rest_array_intersect_key_recursive(), which calls array_intersect_key() without ensuring the value is an array. When WP_REST_Response::get_data() is a stdClass (seen with /wp/v2/taxonomies?type={post_type}&_fields=…), PHP throws:

TypeError: array_intersect_key(): Argument #1 ($array) must be of type array, stdClass given
in wp-includes/rest-api.php (_rest_array_intersect_key_recursive)
Related: for slug-keyed collections such as /wp/v2/taxonomies and /wp/v2/types, _fields intersects top-level keys (taxonomy/type slugs) with field names (name, slug, …), so a successful response is often an empty array [] even when taxonomies exist. Filtering should be applied per item in the collection.

== Steps to reproduce
Site on PHP 8.0+ with at least one public custom post type that has a REST-visible taxonomy (e.g. CPT UI testimonial + testimonial_category), or any setup that yields object-shaped taxonomy collection data for a type filter.
While logged in (or with sufficient caps), open or request:
GET /wp-json/wp/v2/taxonomies?type=testimonial&_fields=name,slug,rest_base,hierarchical,types
(Substitute any post type slug that has associated taxonomies.)

Observe HTTP 500 and the TypeError above in the error log.
Also compare:

`GET /wp-json/wp/v2/taxonomies`
`GET /wp-json/wp/v2/taxonomies?_fields=name,slug,types,rest_base`

The second often returns [] even though the first returns a non-empty object keyed by taxonomy slug.

== Expected behavior
No fatal.
_fields returns a trimmed representation of each taxonomy in the collection.
Non-array response data is coerced to an array (or skipped) before array_intersect_key().
Actual behavior
Uncaught TypeError in _rest_array_intersect_key_recursive() when data is stdClass.

== Environment
WordPress 6.x / 7.x (reproduced with current rest_filter_response_fields / _rest_array_intersect_key_recursive)
PHP 8.x (strict types on array_intersect_key())
Triggered from the block editor / CPT UI (User-Agent: node) hitting the taxonomies endpoint after editing a CPT
Code pointer
wp-includes/rest-api.php:

rest_filter_response_fields()
_rest_array_intersect_key_recursive() — assumes $array1 is always an array
rest_api_default_filters() re-registers rest_filter_response_fields on rest_api_init.

== Suggested fix
Guard/coerce in _rest_array_intersect_key_recursive() / rest_filter_response_fields():

{{{#!php
<?php
if ( is_object( $data ) ) {
    $data = get_object_vars( $data ); // or recursive array cast
}
if ( ! is_array( $data ) ) {
    return $response;
}
}}}

For non-numeric collections whose values are arrays/objects and whose keys are not in the _fields list, apply _rest_array_intersect_key_recursive() to each item (same idea as the wp_is_numeric_array() branch).

summary: Bump minimum PHP version to 8.*
_description:
This ticket tracks discussion and work on the next bump to the minimum PHP version to v8.0 or higher.


== Policy / Criteria for Version Bumps (by @justlevine)

There is **no official policy or criteria** [[https://core.trac.wordpress.org/ticket/58719#comment:30|(ref)]] for handling PHP Version bumps. Pending [[https://core.trac.wordpress.org/ticket/58719#comment:1|that discussion]], the following is based on the processes used until now:

1. Matt is the ultimate decision maker on whether to bump the minimum PHP version.
2. That discussion is initiated by the release/project leads based on several (public and private) factors.
3. A **general** litmus test to gauge whether a version should be bumped is if the % of users (via https://wordpress.org/about/stats/) left behind by the bump is `< 5%`.
4. However, usage stats alone are not reason to bump the minimum PHP Version but also have a positive impact on the project/codebase/tooling/etc.

**Important:** Bumping the minimum PHP version (this ticket) is not the same as changing the [[https://wordpress.org/about/requirements/|minimum ''recommended'' version]] (v8.3 as of 10 Jan 2026).

Background: #62622, #58719, #51043, #57345


== Data Points
Since many years @samiamnot has monthly put the stats updates in comments of the old tickets - see backgroound above. We can continue on this ticket with tracking the appropriate data.

The Stats projection page of @johnbillion [[https://johnbillion.github.io/wp-stats/php.html|can be found here]].

**Note**: .org Stats do not offer a cross-reference between WP/PHP versions. As such these percentages include sites that may already be (colloquially) abandoned on a previous WordPress release,but could theoretically upgrade if their plugin/theme stack supports recent WP versions.

Bumping the minimum version to v8.0 would allow us to remove a lot PHP 7.* compatibility code. The work for this release could be bigger then usual so we should communicate early for when this is planned to be set.


== Projection
This could take quite some time to get below the 5% threshold. Currently as of January 2026 it sits on 22.1%. We'll see how fast it can come down.

An important comment in my view from @jrf about the big effort in maintaining WP running PHP cross-version see #58719. Hopefully we can find some other supportive measures to make users more aware that an upgrade is needed - but thats for another ticket. For the moment lets keep discussions here on how to get to 8.0 and have a space to track usage by @samiamnot 


== Previously
#62622 Bumping the minimum PHP version to 7.4 in WordPress 7.0
#58719 Bumping the minimum PHP version to 7.2 in WordPress 6.6
#57345 Bumping the minimum PHP version to 7.0 in WordPress 6.3
#46594 Bumping the minimum PHP version to 5.6 in WordPress 5.2
#16917 Bumping the minimum PHP version to 5.2 in WordPress 3.2

Protect wp-content/upgrade-temp-backup (and wp-content/upgrade) from being served over HTTP
_description:
I reported this to the WordPress security team as HackerOne #3993590. John closed it as N/A — not a vulnerability — and said I was welcome to open it here, with the caveat that even a bug report might not really apply, and that a Site Health check could help. So this is a hardening request. Rollback stays.

== What happens ==

Since 6.3, every plugin/theme update moves the previous copy into `wp-content/upgrade-temp-backup/{plugins,themes}/<slug>/` (`WP_Upgrader::move_to_temp_backup_dir()`, `@since 6.3.0`). Unpack staging lives in `wp-content/upgrade/`. Both directories sit in the docroot. `mkdir()` does not drop an `index.php` stub or an `.htaccess`. Core already writes `index.php` (`// Silence is golden.`) into `wp-content/`, `wp-content/plugins/`, `wp-content/themes/`, and `wp-content/uploads/`.

Site Health only checks that the temp-backup directory is writable (`update_temp_backup_writable`). It does not check whether leftovers are web-reachable.

Related: #51857, [55720] (path moved from `upgrade/temp-backup/` to `upgrade-temp-backup/`). See also #64510 (open) — leftovers not deleted when the filesystem is used without `WP_Filesystem` credentials. That ticket is about cleanup. This one is about the copy being HTTP-reachable while it exists.

== What I measured ==

* Healthy update, not a crash: Query Monitor 3.20.2 → 4.0.7. The complete previous version (165 files) was HTTP-reachable for about 2.5 seconds, then deleted on shutdown. The weekly cleanup cron cannot cover this window — it exists on every update.
* Leftovers when cleanup does not run: a failed Forminator auto-update left the previous version (1.35.0) answering HTTP 200 for nine days (`forminator.php` + `readme.txt`). WP-Cron was not firing on that site. `readme.txt` discloses the exact vintage.
* Direct PHP execution: on an nginx + php-fpm origin, a planted `.php` under that path returned 200 and ran. Plugin bootstraps that guard on `ABSPATH` no-op on a direct hit; self-contained handlers (file managers, sanitizers, uploaders) do run. Path-keyed WAF rules aimed at `/wp-content/plugins/<slug>/` miss this URL.

I am not claiming a CVE. Execution is conditional. Version/source disclosure of the previous copy is the thing that always happens while the copy exists.

== What I'd like core to consider ==

Cheapest first:

1. Drop the same `index.php` stub core already uses, when these directories are created. Stops listing. Does not stop a direct file request.
2. Drop an `.htaccess` deny (`Require all denied` / `RedirectMatch 404`) next to it, for Apache and LiteSpeed. nginx still needs a vhost rule.
3. A Site Health check for leftover copies in `upgrade-temp-backup/` — the idea John floated.

I already deny both paths at nginx on my own sites (`location ^~`). Default installs get nothing.

Happy to write a patch for (1) and (3) if this is wanted.

summary: render_block_core_template_part / get_404_template is called when in any admin area
_description:
it seems that no matter where you are in the admin area, render_block_core_template_part is invoked. I have no idea why this would be required when in the reading settings area, for example.

to replicate:
1. add error log to render_block_core_template_part like so:

{{{#!php

<?php
/**
 * Server-side rendering of the `core/template-part` block.
 *
 * @package WordPress
 */

 */
function render_block_core_template_part( $attributes ) {
	static $seen_ids = array();

	error_log('WHY IS THIS RENDERING ' . print_r($attributes, true));
	$template_part_id = null;
	$content          = null;
...
}}}

2. check error log, observe that header and footer template parts are there.

This is on the 2025 theme, with no other plugins installed.

Digging deeper:
It appears that in template-loader.php, when on any admin area, get_404_template is invoked... because is_404 is true, because the main query sees {{{$query_vars['p']}}} is empty, because we're not viewing a post.

So a bit more involved than I originally thought.

UPDATE: this was due to the site i was working on missing the file for the site favicon. in fetching the missing favicon, it was rendering the 404 template somewhere else. 

it's still rendering though, and it appears to be a browser plugin request. Using React Developer Tools extension attempts to look for /wp-admin/installHook.js.map, which doesn't exist, triggering the rendering of the 404 page template.

background: a block i'm working on does some complicated stuff, so I was looking to implement a simple caching / transient system to store the rendered output. This entails having a way to flush the cache - but while I was testing it in a custom admin area, there was one block transient that just wouldn't go away. as it turns out, that block was in the header template, and because of my missing favicon image, was getting invoked every time the admin area loaded, and then re-caching the block as it rendered a 404 for the favicon request. neat!

tldr: feels like 404 page templates shouldn't be rendered for requests like these, seems like a lot of extra stuff going on that doesn't need to be.

summary: Enqueue the classic theme styles synced from Gutenberg instead of `classic-themes.css`
_description:
`wp-includes/css/classic-themes.css` is needed to provide the default styles of some core blocks, such as the Button block, in classic themes without a `theme.json`.

Gutenberg has the same styles in [https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/blob/trunk/packages/block-library/src/classic.scss classic.scss], and its build output is already synced to core as `wp-includes/css/dist/block-library/classic.css`, but this file is never loaded. Instead, core enqueues its own copy, which is outdated compared to Gutenberg and is missing the styles for the Tabs and Accordion blocks ([https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/73608 GB 73608]), [https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/77607 GB 77607]).

== Proposed changes

Remove the file bundled in core, and enqueue the stylesheet synced from Gutenberg as `classic-theme-styles` instead. This way, future changes to the styles will reach core through the regular package sync.

Connectors API: document the `type` argument of WP_Connector_Registry::register()
_description:
`WP_Connector_Registry::register()` documents one value for `type`, `ai_provider`, which is special-cased: the key is handed to the PHP AI Client and validated on save, and reset when validation fails (https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/13031 describes the re-validation). A non-generative AI service, one that returns probabilities and confidence rather than text, cannot pass that validation, so registering it as `ai_provider` would clear a working key.

https://core.trac.wordpress.org/ticket/64791 established that plugin-defined types are intended (its use cases include "add a non-AI connector"), and that works: registering under a type of one's own renders the card in its own group on Settings › Connectors, the key is stored and masked by core, and it resolves with the usual env/constant/option precedence. Two gaps remain:

 1. The `register()` docblock still reads as if `ai_provider` were the vocabulary: `@type string $type Required. The connector type, e.g. 'ai_provider'.` Nothing states that other values are supported or how the Connectors screen treats them.

 2. An AI service outside the AI Client is neither `ai_provider` nor a plain non-AI service, and there is no name for it. Each such plugin invents a type, and the screen groups by type, so two judgement-model connectors from two authors would land under two headings. A documented core value (`ai_service`, or whatever name fits) would let them group together, and would give the AI plugin something to recognise when it decides whether AI credentials exist.

Ask: document that plugin-defined types are supported, and add or name one for AI services the AI Client does not drive.

Working example: https://github.com/juanlentino/jev-connector, registered as `ai_decision`, verified on 7.1. Companion request on the PHP AI Client side, for a capability that would let such models be first-class there: https://github.com/WordPress/php-ai-client/issues/296.

REST API: Template and template part collections fetch every template again to build its links
_description:
`WP_REST_Templates_Controller::prepare_item_for_response()` passes only the template ID to `prepare_links()`. When the post type supports revisions, `prepare_links()` calls `get_block_template()` for every item, only to read `wp_id` for the revision links (added in [56819], #56922). That is another `WP_Query` per item, and for theme file templates another file read and Block Hooks pass, and the result is discarded.

Measured on 7.2-beta1 with Ipsum, as admin, `rest_do_request()`, median of 5:

|| '''Endpoint''' || '''Queries''' || '''Time''' ||
|| `/wp/v2/template-parts` (8 items) || 9 to 1 || 12.7 to 6.5 ms ||
|| `/wp/v2/templates` (11 items) || 17 to 6 || 23.3 to 17.2 ms ||

The patch hands the template that is being prepared to `prepare_links()` through a private property, so the `prepare_links( $id )` signature stays the same for subclasses, and falls back to `get_block_template()` otherwise. summary: Improve clarity of REST API meta field error message "The %s property has an invalid stored value, and cannot be updated to null."

This message could be displayed to end user(e.g. in the block editor)

**Current message**:


{{{
"The %s property has an invalid stored value, and cannot be updated to null."
}}}


**Related Files**:

- [wp-includes/rest-api/endpoints/class-wp-rest-settings-controller.php#L208](https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/ebd415b045a2b1bbeb4d227e890c78a15ff8d85e/src/wp-includes/rest-api/endpoints/class-wp-rest-settings-controller.php#L208)

**Issues**:

1. Unclear what "property" refers to (meta field? custom field?)
2. Doesn't explain what makes the value invalid
3. No guidance on how to fix the issue

**Proposed improvement**:

{{{
'The field "%s" contains an invalid value, and cannot be updated. Please enter a valid value or contact your site administrator.'
}}}

This message is used in 2 different controllers, so it's also possible to make variations for each class:

- For settings controller: 'The setting "%s" contains an invalid value...'
- For meta fields: 'The meta field "%s" contains an invalid value...'

**Related Issues:**

Gutenberg #17864: "Saving a certain meta key saves other unmodified keys" https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/issues/17864

summary: Abilities API: explore allowing an ability to belong to multiple categories
_description:
Tracking ticket from the #core-ai chat: explore support for multiple categories per ability.

== Current behaviour ==

An ability must declare exactly one category, and it is required:

{{{#!php
// wp-includes/abilities-api/class-wp-ability.php
if ( empty( $args['category'] ) || ! is_string( $args['category'] ) ) {
	// "The ability properties must contain a `category` string."
}
}}}

That single slug then flows through the whole API surface:

 * `WP_Ability::get_category(): string` returns one slug.
 * `WP_Abilities_Registry::register()` rejects an ability whose category is not already registered.
 * `wp_get_abilities( array( 'category' => 'content' ) )` keeps an ability only when `$ability->get_category() === $category` — an exact, single match.
 * REST: `wp-abilities/v1/abilities` exposes `category` as a `string` response field and accepts a single-string `category` collection parameter (sanitised with `sanitize_key`); `wp-abilities/v1/categories` links each category to `…/abilities?category=<slug>`.

== Why this is limiting ==

Plenty of abilities genuinely sit in more than one bucket — generating alt text for an attachment is both "media" and "content"; exporting users to CSV is both "users" and "data export". Today the registrant has to pick one, and the fact that it also belongs elsewhere is simply lost.

Because the category is the only first-class grouping dimension, every consumer that groups or filters abilities inherits that lossiness: the Abilities Explorer, MCP tool grouping in the MCP Adapter, command-palette-style UIs. Discovery degrades — the ability is invisible under a category a user would reasonably browse. Consumers route around it with naming conventions or private `meta`, which fragments across plugins instead of being solved once in core.

== Questions to settle ==

1. **Shape.** Widen `category` to accept `string|string[]`, or add a separate plural argument (e.g. `categories`) while `category` stays the single canonical/primary one? The latter keeps a stable "which one do I display" answer for UIs and preserves back-compat for everything reading `get_category()`.
2. **Back-compat.** `get_category(): string` has a scalar return type and cannot change. Add `get_categories(): array` alongside it, with `get_category()` continuing to return the primary?
3. **Filtering semantics.** `wp_get_abilities( array( 'category' => 'x' ) )` should presumably match when `x` is any of the ability's categories. Should it also accept a list, and if so is that OR or AND?
4. **REST.** Add a `categories` array field to the abilities schema (keeping `category` for back-compat), and decide whether the `category` collection parameter accepts multiple slugs — it is string-only today.
5. **Still required?** Keep "at least one category" mandatory so discovery stays guaranteed, rather than allowing an empty list.
6. **Downstream.** Impact on the MCP Adapter's grouping and on the Abilities Explorer UI.
7. **Right model?** Is a flat multi-category list the correct answer, or is the real request tags/taxonomy alongside a single primary category?

== Related ==

 * #64345 — ability names should support versioning
 * #64209 — allow abilities to be deprecated

Both touch the same registration-shape surface.

Position block support: derive container class from styles so identical rules are deduplicated
_description:
`wp_render_position_support()` builds its container class from a per-request counter:

{{{#!php
<?php
$class_name = wp_unique_id( 'wp-container-' );
}}}

Every block instance with position support therefore gets its own class and its own rule in the `block-supports` style engine store, even when the resulting CSS is byte-for-byte identical.

The other block supports that emit a scoped rule derive the class from the style inputs, so identical styles collapse into one rule:

||= Support =||= Class strategy =||
|| `layout.php` || `wp_unique_id_from_values( $hash_input, 'wp-container-' )` ||
|| `custom-css.php` || `wp_unique_id_from_values( $parsed_block, ... )` ||
|| `states.php` || `md5()` of the rules ||
|| `settings.php` || `md5( serialize( $block ) )` ||
|| **`position.php`** || **`wp_unique_id()` (counter)** ||

`wp_render_layout_support_flag()` documents why it hashes: to keep class names the same for blocks with the same definition, and stable across paginations such as the Query block's enhanced pagination. Position uses the same `wp-container-` prefix but doesn't get that behaviour.

=== Impact ===

With 200 Group blocks that all use `position: sticky; top: 0px`:

||= =||= Rules in store =||= Generated CSS =||
|| trunk || 200 || 22,092 bytes ||
|| patched || 1 || 116 bytes ||

This CSS is inlined into every front-end response, so the duplication adds page weight on every request, on top of the render cost.

summary: Introduce a REST API endpoint for sites
_description:
It should be possible to manage sites in a multisite configuration through the REST API.

* List sites: `GET wp/v2/sites/`
* Retrieve a site: `GET wp/v2/sites/<id>`
* Create a site: `POST wp/v2/sites/`
* Update a site: `PUT wp/v2/sites/<id>`
* Delete a site: `DELETE wp/v2/sites/<id>`

Data included in a site object should at least mirror the data available for the site in `wp_blogs`. Additional ideal pieces of data for a site include `blogname`, `blogdescription`, `home`, and `siteurl`. It's possible that creating a new meta table for sites can help developers register meta for inclusion with a site object (See #37923).

Sites should be accessible by default for authenticated users only. Network (global) admins should have access to all sites. Site users should have access to the sites they are members of. The "My Sites" list is a great candidate for exploring how this will work. See #15317.

As of the introduction of `get_sites()` in 4.6.0, retrieving sites is a much better experience. The methods used to create, update, and delete sites in multisite are not as pleasant right now. We should investigate each of these and determine what can be done to streamline the process. The first improvement is probably in creating a site. See #40364.

summary: Plugin update via modal does not update plugins list until page reload
_description:
If you visit the "Plugins" page in the admin section and there is a plugin update available, the following text will be displayed:

  There is a new version of [the plugin's name] available. View version [the plugin's latest version] details or update now.

If you click the "View version ... details" link, a modal dialog box (using an iframe) will be displayed with a button to perform the update.

Before WordPress 6.5, this button was labeled "Install Update Now".  If you clicked the button, the modal would close, the text on the main page would change to "Updating..." and then finally this text would change to "Updated!" when the update was completed.

In WordPress 6.5 and later, the button is labeled "Update Now" (and has a different appearance).  If you click the button, the modal does not close, but the text on the button changes to "Updating..." and then finally "Updated!"  If you close the modal, you will see that the main page has not changed at all: the plugin still displays the old version with the same "There is a new version of [the plugin's name] available..." text.  You have to manually reload the page in order to see that the plugin has been updated to the new version.

Is this behavior intentional?  Probably the change in the button label and appearance was intentional (but that's not very important).  Keeping the modal open during the update might be intentional (although I preferred the old behavior).  But failing to update the main page seems like a bug, or at least a significant regression in functionality compared to earlier versions.

summary: Introduce a CSS tokenizer.
_description:
Many operations within WordPress need to process CSS content, whether inline `style` elements with their list of declarations, `STYLE` element CSS, or `theme.json`-like CSS-inside-JSON.

Currently, code tends to run naive PCRE patterns against the CSS. This presents a number of common problems related to string values, basic tokenization, and the like.

WordPress could use at least a CSS lexer which would allow code to speak at the level of language tokens instead of repeating the same overly-simplific parsers in different places, leaving opportunity for parsing differentials or misparses.

summary: get_plugins() cache ignores extra_plugin_headers registered after the first scan
_description:
`get_plugins()` stores plugin headers in the `plugins` object cache on the first scan. `get_file_data()` applies `extra_plugin_headers` only while that scan reads files. A later `get_plugins()` hits the cache and never sees headers registered in between.

That first scan often happens during plugin include, before `plugins_loaded`. Any plugin that calls `get_plugins()` there freezes a snapshot with no extra headers. Plugins that register extra headers and then read them get empty values, notices on missing keys, or skip their own update logic.

=== Reproduction ===

1. Plugin A, slug sorting before plugin B, calls `get_plugins()` in the main file (include time).
2. Plugin B adds a header on `extra_plugin_headers` and later calls `get_plugins()`.
3. Plugin B's extra header key is missing from the cached rows.

`get_plugins( '/some-slug' )` is a separate cache slot today, so a folder scan does not reuse a warm all-plugins list and can freeze the same stale headers on its own key.

=== Expected ===

Extra headers registered after the first scan should appear on the next `get_plugins()` call. Already-cached fields (Name, Version, ...) should stay. A folder argument should scan only that folder. `SHORTINIT` should not prime this cache; only `get_plugins()` should fill it.

=== Seen in the wild ===

[https://github.com/sybrew/troy/issues/24 Troy Client #24]. Troy Client registers custom plugin headers and uses them to talk to Troy Server and to keep Troy plugins off wordpress.org's update-check. An early `get_plugins()` meant those headers never landed, so Client could not see its own plugins. Client 1.8.1184 flushes the cache as a workaround. Core should not require that.

WooCommerce has hit the same cache for years. The Helper needs a `Woo:` extra header to see paid extensions (subscriptions and Woo.com updates). `WC tested up to` / `WC requires at least` also vanish, so extensions look untested. Woo already flushes `wp_cache` group `plugins` when those keys are missing (WooCommerce PRs: [https://github.com/woocommerce/woocommerce/pull/26358 #26358], [https://github.com/woocommerce/woocommerce/pull/21669 #21669]). That is a product workaround for this core bug. They knew about the bug, so I'm surprised that they didn't raise an issue with WordPress.

Plugin authors should not have to detect missing keys and flush the `plugins` cache themselves. A core fix does that work once. Sites that update WordPress then see extra headers on the next `get_plugins()` call, so custom update-server connections this cache bug severed start working again without a plugin update.

Themes cannot cause this. They load after `plugins_loaded`.

summary: Block Hooks: Skip parsing and re-serializing post content in the_content when no blocks are hooked
_description:
Pages with a lot of block content are slow because, since 6.8, every the_content call parses and re-serializes the whole post even when no block is hooked, and the per-block Block Hooks visitors run on top of that.

[58291] ([https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/commit/b39f58ec3eab0f2b66dccebbf0fc97baaaaa9a15 b39f58ec]) returned early from apply_block_hooks_to_content() when nothing was hooked.
[59101] ([https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/commit/2952e563aae229fe497e723996cc5a58b92e1401 2952e563], #61902) removed that early return so template parts still get the theme attribute. Parsing and serializing now always run, and the has_filter( 'hooked_block_types' ) check only selects the visitors ([https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/0004f4d2e149e41dab07cfdf3e019f4a96cb4e06/src/wp-includes/blocks.php#L1171 blocks.php:1171]).
[60173] ([https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/commit/e800c60ec09a06cf73407f992d7ed1352e3c3973 e800c60e], #63287, in 6.8.1) added a temporary hooked_block_types filter inside apply_block_hooks_to_content_from_post_object() ([https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/0004f4d2e149e41dab07cfdf3e019f4a96cb4e06/src/wp-includes/blocks.php#L1354-L1356 blocks.php:1354-1356]). That filter makes the has_filter() check always true on this path, so the per-block visitors always run.
The PRs for [60173] ([https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/8695 8695], [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/8700 8700]) do not mention this, and it appears to be unintended.

Timing apply_block_hooks_to_content_from_post_object() on ~1 MB of block markup with nothing hooked (PHP 8.4):

trunk: 34-35 ms per call
with the patch: 0.4 ms per call
=== Steps to reproduce ===

In the PHPUnit test environment on trunk [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/commit/0004f4d2e149e41dab07cfdf3e019f4a96cb4e06 0004f4d2], with no plugins and no hooked blocks, create a post with ~1 MB of nested paragraph, group and columns blocks.
Time repeated calls of apply_block_hooks_to_content_from_post_object( $post->post_content, $post ).
Expected: the content is not parsed when nothing is hooked. Actual: it is parsed and re-serialized on every call.
=== Proposed fix ===

Return the content unchanged at the top of apply_block_hooks_to_content_from_post_object(), before the temporary filter is added, when:

get_hooked_blocks() is empty and has_filter( 'hooked_block_types' ) is false;
has_block( 'core/template-part', $content ) is false;
$ignored_hooked_blocks_at_root is null (REST passes an empty array, which keeps the full path, #65008).
Output is unchanged for well-formed content. Content with a stray closing delimiter renders as it did before 6.8. (Since 6.8, the temporary wrapper block has been making the parser recover and render those broken blocks anyway, and the patch removes that recovery whenever it skips the pass.)

The patch adds one test, test_apply_block_hooks_to_content_from_post_object_returns_content_unchanged_if_no_hooked_blocks, to applyBlockHooksToContentFromPostObject.php. Run with php vendor/bin/phpunit --group block-hooks (SQLite).

AI disclosure:
AI assistance: Yes
Tool(s): Claude Code, Codex CLI
Model(s): Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra
Used for: root-cause analysis, git history checks, patch, test and benchmark drafting, accuracy review; 
I reviewed the patch and the claims.

_description:
The `$postarr` value passed to the `wp_insert_post()` function contains context that can be useful to callbacks attached to the actions that fire within this function, but this value isn't passed to any of them. Strangely enough it ''is'' passed to most of the filters there.

As an example, a plugin of mine needs to perform logic within a callback on the `wp_insert_post` action based on a mixture of the `tax_input` argument and a custom argument. The `wp_insert_post_data` filter needs to be used to access these values.

The `$postarr` value gets copied to `$unsanitized_postarr`. This is the value that should be passed to the actions because it contains the original input array, rather than `$postarr` which includes defaults and sanitised values. Or both should be passed, as per the filters in the function.

This affects the following actions:

summary: Lazy load user capabilities in WP_User object
_description:
WP_User object are used throughout WordPress and are loaded on the front end [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/907eb2893f331f5d9cda1f277d3dd3137deb0f50/src/wp-includes/class-wp-query.php#L4715 in WP_Query]. This means creating a WP_User object and this calls `for_site` method. This calls to user meta and setups capability data. For a page with multiple users on it, this setup of users, can be done multiple times. Loading user meta for all the users, can be a problem, as this can be a lot of rows of data. For example, this can result in 150 rows being loaded from the database for just 10 users. For multisites or sites that have plugins that are heavy users of user meta, that number can get much higher. 

User meta is only loaded along with users, as it is needed for capability data. To improve performance, find someway to lazy load the capability only when they are used and also lazily load user meta at the same time.

summary: Cache file sizes of core block style files.
_description: Introduced in #58528 / [56044], there is now cache for file lookups for core block styles. This was to save file lookups and improve server response time. As there is already an existing transient cache, reuse that to also cache the file size of the files.

Plugin dependencies: better messaging or management of plugin active states
_description:
Currently, if a plugin cannot be deleted due to plugin dependencies, it has a single message that shows "Note: This plugin cannot be deactivated or deleted until the plugins that require it are deactivated or deleted."

The message is inaccurate in two ways - you cannot delete a plugin unless the plugins that require it are deleted; deactivating is not sufficient; and it does not reflect the current state of the plugin. If the plugin with dependents is already deactivated, it still states that it cannot be deactivated.

Much of the structure of plugin dependencies seems to ignore whether a referenced plugin is active or not.

The checks are dependent on `get_dependent_names()`, which does not contain any reference to whether or not a plugin is active.

At minimum, the messages should be improved so that they accurately reflect what needs to happen; alternately, the messages and states should be matched so that the possible scenarios are reflected more accurately.

summary: first class callable syntax support in _wp_filter_build_unique_id() / remove_filter()
_description:
PHP 8.1 introduced something called "First class callable" or First-class Callable Syntax - [https://www.php.net/releases/8.1/en.php#first_class_callable_syntax]

Which basically means much easier way to reference any function, especially class methods - both dynamic and static like so:

{{{
$this->myDynamicCallback(...);
self::myStaticCallback(...);
}}}
''**The 3 dots "..." are not omission - it is the syntax**''

Now this syntax actually works for `add_filter` however, it can fail (and I've encountered cases where it fails) for `remove_filter` which leads to very unexpected results.

Temporary bypass can be done using `remove_all_filters` or the old-school syntax `[__CLASS__, 'myStaticCallback']`.

The core issue is in the function `_wp_filter_build_unique_id` which generates the key under which the callback is stored, more specifically, in the way how the PHP's `spl_object_hash` work - this sentence from docs "This id can be used as a hash key for storing objects, or for identifying an object, **as long as the object is not destroyed**."

Now this is an educated wild guess, but I would guess that the callable objects created by the First-class callable syntax may not live that long and garbage collector can destroy them if it sees fit.

Anyways... the core is - `spl_object_hash` is NOT the right tool to cache ALL callables, but can only be used where the callable is passed around (e.g. stored in a variable) and therefore it is ensured it's still the same object (I would hope).

**Solution**
...for such cases is to create a `\ReflectionFunction` instance and check for `getClosureScopeClass()` and `getName()` :-)

https://www.php.net/manual/en/class.reflectionfunction.php
https://www.php.net/manual/en/reflectionfunctionabstract.getclosurescopeclass.php
https://www.php.net/manual/en/reflectionfunctionabstract.getname.php

Expand the Tools screen with Import, Export, and Code Editing cards & adding a message when there are no tools to display
_description:
The Tools screen currently shows a single card, the Categories and Tags Converter,
even though Tools is the home of Import, Export and — for block themes — the Theme
and Plugin File Editors. Users have to already know those screens exist in the submenu.

This adds three cards in the existing `.card` style used by the converter, each
listing the options available on its screen and linking to it:

 * '''Import Tools''' — the importers returned by {{{wp_get_popular_importers()}}}, shown only to users who can {{{install_plugins}}} (matching import.php)
 * '''Export Tools''' — the choices offered by export.php, including any custom post type registered with {{{can_export}}}
 * '''Code Editing Tools''' — Theme File Editor and Plugin File Editor

Each card is gated independently on the capability its target screen enforces
({{{import}}}, {{{export}}}, {{{edit_themes}}}, {{{edit_plugins}}}), so the screen only
advertises what the user can actually reach. The Plugin File Editor entry follows
menu.php and is hidden on multisite, and the Code Editing card disappears entirely
under {{{DISALLOW_FILE_EDIT}}}.

When nothing at all renders — including nothing hooked to {{{tool_box}}} — the screen
shows "No tools are available for your account." instead of being blank.

== Relationship to #42486 ==

This resolves the blank Tools screen reported in #42486, but by filling the page
rather than by removing the menu item.

The patches on that ticket all hide the Tools menu when it would be empty. That
approach stalled because hiding Tools breaks plugins that add submenus for users
without {{{import}}} (comment 48), and because of the capability asymmetry dd32
listed in comment 4 (can import but not export, and vice versa). Per-card gating
handles both. Filling the page was suggested on that ticket by dd32 in comment 4
and by Clorith in comment 38.

Note this deliberately keeps the Tools menu item. If this lands, the menu.php change
proposed in #42486 may no longer be needed, but that is a separate decision and this
patch does not touch menu.php.

== Backward compatibility ==

{{{tool_box}}} fires unchanged — same name, no arguments, same position. Its output is
buffered only so that a plugin card suppresses the empty-state message; the output is
echoed unmodified.

The Categories and Tags Converter card, its markup and its help tab id are unchanged.

Three new filters let plugins adjust or remove each new card:

 * {{{tools_screen_import_options}}}
 * {{{tools_screen_export_options}}}
 * {{{tools_screen_code_editing_options}}}

Happy to drop these if new hooks are not wanted; the cards work without them.

== Strings ==

Four new strings: "Import Tools", "Export Tools", "Code Editing Tools" and "No tools
are available for your account." Everything else reuses existing translations — the
editor descriptions come from theme-editor.php and plugin-editor.php, the export list
from export.php, and the importer names and descriptions from
{{{wp_get_popular_importers()}}}.

== Testing ==

 * Administrator: all four cards
 * {{{export}}} but not {{{import}}} or file editing: only the Export card
 * Author/Contributor: the "No tools are available for your account." message
 * Author/Contributor with a plugin hooked to {{{tool_box}}}: the plugin card renders, no message
 * A custom post type with {{{can_export => true}}} appears in the Export list; {{{can_export => false}}} does not
